s: People Poddle People Archbishops and rebels, millers and nuns, a dean, a spy and a playwright’s father: the people whose lives ran alongside the river. Each links to the places on the walk and in the history where their story is told.

died 2006 · The first Poddleologist A Dominican nun from Blackrock who taught at Muckross Park in Donnybrook, Sister Ann made the Poddle her cause. She traced it on foot through the Liberties, falling in twice along the way, photographed stretches that were about to vanish, and argued that its meeting with the Liffey formed the Dubh Linn that gave the city its name. She coined the word “Poddleologist” for anyone who follows the river. In the early 1970s she campaigned against the building over of the City Watercourse at Templeogue, frustrated by what she saw as apathy and poor planning, and won the support of Seán Rothery, chairman of An Taisce. She wrote the narration for John Gleeson’s 16mm film of the watercourse, led walks along the river for the 1973 Dublin Arts Festival, and wrote “Down the Old Poddle” for The Liberties of Dublin (1973). She died on 10 March 2006. On poddle.ie: Saving the watercourse · “An underground river!” · Willington and the watercourse · Her walk to Warrenmount

1572–1602 · Escaped from Dublin Castle by the river Heir to the O’Donnells of Tír Chonaill, Red Hugh was kidnapped at fifteen in 1587, lured aboard a ship at Rathmullan, and held in Dublin Castle as a hostage. A first escape in 1590 failed. At Christmas 1591 he and Henry and Art O’Neill got free of their fetters, let themselves down by a rope into the Poddle where it ran under the Castle, crossed the moat and fled into the Wicklow mountains in deep snow. Art O’Neill died of cold, and Red Hugh lost his big toes to frostbite before the O’Byrnes of Glenmalure brought them to safety. He went on to lead the Nine Years’ War with Hugh O’Neill. On poddle.ie: The moat and the escape

1688–1768 · Held the city’s water to ransom Sir Thomas Domville took Templeogue House after the Talbots lost it in 1688, and with it control of the City Watercourse that crossed his land. His son Sir Compton Domville made the watercourse the centrepiece of his gardens, and is remembered for using it as a weapon: when his nephew Lord Santry was condemned for killing a tavern porter in 1739, Sir Compton is said to have threatened to cut off the city’s water unless Santry was spared. Santry was pardoned. The story is famous, though how much the threat decided it is debated. On poddle.ie: Guarding the water · Templeogue House

mayor 1302–1324 · The mayor who built the city’s fountain Six times mayor of Dublin (1302, 1305, 1307 to 1309 and 1324), Le Decer paid for public works himself. In 1308 he had the watercourse cleaned and faced with stone, and built a marble cistern at Cornmarket, by St Audoen’s, fed from the City Watercourse. People called it Le Decer’s fountain, or the High Pipe. Tradition says he set the “Lucky Stone”, an early grave slab, beside it, and that whoever drank there had good luck. On poddle.ie: Rebuilding the watercourse · Water for the city

1667–1745 · Dean of St Patrick’s, on the river’s island Jonathan Swift, painted by Charles Jervas, 1710. Wikimedia Commons , public domain Swift was Dean of St Patrick’s from 1713 until his death, in a cathedral built on an island between two streams of the Poddle, with the water a few feet beneath its floor. He opposed a plan to crown its tower with a brick spire. One account says the Poddle Guard was set up in 1725 to stop him rousing the crowds of the Liberties against the government; others say it simply policed the rough ground by the cathedral. He left most of his fortune to found St Patrick’s Hospital, which still cares for patients today. On poddle.ie: A cathedral on wet ground · The Poddle Guard

1725–1803 · Brewed with the City Watercourse On 31 December 1759 Arthur Guinness took a lease of the disused brewery at St James’s Gate from Mark Rainsford, for 9,000 years at £45 a year. The lease gave him free use of “the said Pipe water or City Water Course”, the water the City Watercourse carried down from the Dodder and the Poddle to the City Basin beside the brewery. When Dublin Corporation came with the Sheriff in May 1775 to fill in his channel, he took a pickaxe from one of the workmen and told them the water was his and he would defend it. The quarrel ended in a compromise in the mid-1780s, when he agreed to pay £10 a year for the water. On poddle.ie: Arthur Guinness’s lease · The pickaxe, 1775 · The City Basin

1798–1868 · Restored St Patrick’s on its island Sir Benjamin Lee Guinness, painted by Stephen Catterson Smith the younger, 1862–3. Wikimedia Commons , public domain Arthur Guinness’s grandson ran the brewery and was Lord Mayor of Dublin in 1851. Between 1860 and 1865 he paid for the great restoration of St Patrick’s Cathedral, when it was feared the building, standing on wet ground between two streams of the Poddle, might collapse. His statue stands outside the cathedral. On poddle.ie: Out of sight · The Guinness family by the Poddle

1847–1927 · Rebuilt the Poddle valley Edward Cecil Guinness, 1st Earl of Iveagh, photographer and date unknown. Wikimedia Commons , public domain The third son of Sir Benjamin Lee Guinness, Edward Cecil Guinness ran the brewery and was made Lord Iveagh in 1891. Around 1900 the streets between St Patrick’s and Bride Street, the “Poddle valley”, were some of the worst slums in the city, with houses sinking into the river beneath them. Lord Iveagh cleared them and laid out St Patrick’s Park, opened in 1902, and his Iveagh Trust built the Bull Alley flats (1901 to 1906), the Iveagh Hostel and the Iveagh Baths on Bride Road (1906), and the Iveagh Play Centre (1915). He also paid for the Iveagh Markets on Francis Street. The Corporation moved part of the river to give the new buildings firm ground, and in 1902 thanked him for a gift of £1,400 towards completing the new channel from the cathedral to where the two branches met. During the works of 1901 the old carved stone thought to mark St Patrick’s Well was found in the culvert beside the cathedral. On poddle.ie: Out of sight · The Iveagh Buildings · St Patrick’s Well · The Guinness family by the Poddle · Guinness workers at Blackpitts

1814–1885 · The playwright’s father, a reluctant miller Born in Kilkenny, a civil servant who sold his pension for £500 and went into the flour trade, George Carr Shaw ran Rutland mill on the City Watercourse with his partner Clibborn. His son, George Bernard Shaw, described a business that “did not work the industry: it worked them”, and his father laughing helplessly in an empty corner of the warehouse after a customer’s bankruptcy all but ruined them. The mill kept him until he died in 1885. On poddle.ie: Shaw’s mill, Rutland Avenue · The mills

1799–1876 · Recorder of Dublin, at Kimmage Recorder of Dublin from 1830 to 1876 and MP for the city and then Dublin University, Shaw lived at Kimmage House, on the Poddle, from 1829 until he died. He remodelled it in the Tudor style, built Whitehall Road as its new approach, and married Thomasina Emily Jocelyn, a granddaughter of the Earl of Roden. His granddaughter Flora Shaw named Nigeria. On poddle.ie: Frederick Shaw · From Kimmage House to Kimmage Manor

1914–1916 · Larkfield and the Kimmage Garrison Joseph Mary Plunkett, about 1910, photographer unknown. Wikimedia Commons , public domain Countess Plunkett held the lease of Larkfield, the old mill on the Poddle by Sundrive Road, and her sons, Joseph Mary Plunkett among them, made it a base for the Volunteers: a store for the Howth guns of 1914 and, before Easter 1916, home to the Kimmage Garrison. Joseph Mary Plunkett signed the Proclamation and was executed after the Rising. On poddle.ie: Larkfield Mill and the Kimmage Garrison · Mill country

1181–1228 · Built on the river’s island John Comyn, the first Norman archbishop of Dublin, built his palace of St Sepulchre beside the Poddle and made the little church on its island collegiate in 1191. His successor, Henry de Loundres, raised it to a cathedral, and was granted the manor of Tymon by King John in 1216. On poddle.ie: A cathedral on wet ground · St Sepulchre’s Palace · Tymon estate

1787–1858 · Founded the Hospice on the river Mary Aikenhead as a young woman, about 1807, artist unknown. Wikimedia Commons , public domain Founder of the Religious Sisters of Charity and of St Vincent’s Hospital, she bought Greenmount at Harold’s Cross in 1845, on the banks of the Poddle, and made it the congregation’s mother house. Our Lady’s Hospice grew from it. On poddle.ie: Our Lady’s Hospice · Greenmount and the Hospice

19th century · Quaker mill owners at Greenmount The Quaker Pim family, Thomas, Jonathan and Joseph Robinson Pim of Pim Brothers, enlarged the Greenmount mill on the Poddle into the Greenmount Spinning Company, making cotton, linen and Irish poplin, and were known for their work for better conditions and charity. On poddle.ie: Greenmount

1821–1893 · The healer by the river Father Charles Houben in his Passionist habit, 19th-century photograph. Wikimedia Commons , public domain Charles Houben, a Dutch Passionist, came to the new monastery at Mount Argus in 1857, where the Poddle ran through the grounds. Crowds came to him for healing. He was canonised in 2007. On poddle.ie: Saint Charles · The first Mount Argus

died 1956 · Landlady with washing rights in the Poddle Daughter of the builder Arthur Hammond, she inherited 150 houses around Blackpitts in 1902, many let to Guinness workers, with the right to wash in the River Poddle written into the deeds. She is remembered as a British spy during and after the First World War. On poddle.ie: Washing rights in the Poddle

c. 1794–1846 · The blind rhymer of the Liberties The street balladeer Michael Moran, known as Zozimus, was born in Faddle Alley off Blackpitts and died in Patrick Street, both on the river’s course. A play about him, Zoz, was staged at the Olympia, over the Poddle, in 1975. On poddle.ie: Through the Liberties

1879 · Built a music hall over the river Dan Lowrey opened the Star of Erin music hall on Dame Street in 1879, now the Olympia. The Poddle beneath it decided where the stage went and why the audience still comes in through a tunnel. On poddle.ie: The Olympia and the river

City Surveyor, 1890s–1900s · The engineer who found St Patrick’s Well As Dublin’s Borough Surveyor, Harty dealt with the open river at Donore Avenue and rebuilt the culverts in the Liberties. In June 1901, opening the old arched course of the Poddle in Patrick Street, he found the stone marking St Patrick’s Well. On poddle.ie: Donore Avenue, 1901 · Between two streams

1882–1941 · Put the Poddle in Ulysses James Joyce in Zurich, photographed by Alex Ehrenzweig, 1915. Wikimedia Commons , public domain Joyce gave the river a sentence in Ulysses, misplacing its mouth at Wood Quay: “Poddle river hung out in fealty a tongue of liquid sewage.” On poddle.ie: Ulysses Parts of this page draw on research by the volunteers of the Crumlin and Walkinstown History Group, shared with poddle.ie. t: Dolphin’s Barn and the City Watercourse
s: Meander · off Stop 9, The Stone Boat Dolphin’s Barn and the City Watercourse Follow the third of the water that left at the Stone Boat, past Shaw’s mill and the Back of the Pipes to the City Basin.

From the Stone Boat the City Watercourse ran north-west, between today’s Mount Jerome and Eamonn Ceannt Park, and along Rutland Avenue to Dolphin’s Barn. Rutland Avenue was once Hall’s Lane, and may have been renamed after the 4th Duke of Rutland, Lord Lieutenant from 1784 until he died at the Viceregal Lodge in 1787. Rutland flour mill stood on the watercourse here, on the country side of the canal at the end of what George Bernard Shaw called “a rather pretty little village street”. His father, George Carr Shaw, ran it with a partner, George Clibborn, as Clibborn and Shaw, flour and corn merchants, with an office and warehouse at 67 Jervis Street. In 1938 a newspaper found that the pair had borrowed on the mill, its pond and machinery near Hall’s Lane, and that the ruins of “Shaw’s Mill” could still be seen; one Blackpitts resident remembered the playwright from childhood. Shaw himself wrote that neither partner knew anything about flour, so the business “proceeded by its own momentum”: “They did not work the industry: it worked them.” Rutland Avenue had football too. Jacob’s FC, formed by workers at the Bishop Street biscuit factory, played here, and in 1921 were founder members of the League of Ireland with their neighbours St James’s Gate. Three Jacob’s players were capped for Ireland: Frank Collins, Tommy Dunne and a Crumlin man, Shay Keogh. Show Rutland Avenue on the map →

William Clarke and Son, tobacco and snuff makers, began in South Main Street, Cork, in 1830 and moved production to Liverpool by 1870. When the Irish Free State brought in its own customs duties, the firm came back, and in 1923 and 1924 built a factory at 276 to 288 South Circular Road, on what the old maps show as open fields. Beckett and Harrington designed it with R. Earle, chief engineer of Clarke’s parent, the Imperial Tobacco Company: a single-storey works lit by north lights, then an office building on the road in brick with stone dressings. A staff restaurant followed in 1949, and in the 1960s Player Wills added offices. The Tenter Water, a branch of the City Watercourse, ran by the site. In December 1924 the Dublin Borough Commissioners began a relief scheme, with a £45,000 government grant, to give work to the unemployed. One of its jobs, costing £2,600, was to divert the Poddle into a culvert at Clarke’s new factory, so that its water no longer ran into the sewers or lay stagnant. Show Clarke’s tobacco factory on the map →

In the 19th century Dolphin’s Barn was busy with tanneries and mills. In the 1840s tanners such as James O’Neill, Patrick Ledwidge, Peter Byrne and Margaret Jones worked side by side on Dolphin’s Barn Lane, and the city’s records are full of disputes with tanners over what they did to the water. Better-off residents were allowed to supply their poorer neighbours from private fountains, landlords piped water to tenants through pipes no thicker than a goose quill, and near Kimmage and Dolphin’s Barn people cut holes in the banks to water their fields. The river was dangerous. In August 1877 a child, Eliza McMahon, fell into the Poddle near her home at 20 Rutland Avenue and drowned; the inquest jury asked the Corporation to do something about the state of the river. In September 1931 a boy named Rooney from Rutland Avenue found the body of an infant in it. In March 1937 a grating above Rutland Cottages choked, where the river went underground for 400 yards before it emptied into the canal near Dolphin’s Barn Bridge. Cottages flooded three feet deep. Mrs McNamara of 5 Rutland Cottages spent the night carrying her children to safety, and in the morning made breakfast standing knee-deep in water. In January 1938 Dublin Corporation announced 556 flats for 550 families between Dolphin’s Barn Street and Donore Avenue, a £250,000 scheme that meant widening both streets and diverting the part of the Poddle that ran through the site. Show Dolphin’s Barn on the map →

From Dolphin’s Barn the watercourse was carried on a raised bank to the City Basin. The lane along it, between Dolphin’s Barn and James’s Walk, was known as the Back of the Pipes. It ran behind Reuben Street, Fatima Mansions, Mallin Avenue and Lourdes Road, past the “Stone Sofa”, and came out on James’s Walk opposite the old iron footbridge. For generations it was a place for courting couples, and in Dublin slang anything that could not be found was “at the back of the pipes”. Nearby stood the Leinster cinema, later the Dublin Ice Rink. The line of the old canal branch here was filled in and the Luas now runs along it. In March 1879 the Irish Times reported “a crime of a most fiendish nature”. A woman lured a four-year-old girl from Pill Lane to the Back of the Pipes, stripped her and threw her over a six-foot wall into the Poddle. The river was usually four feet deep and swift, but that day there were only two feet of water; the child stood up and screamed, and a neighbour saved her. Her clothes turned up in a pawn office the next morning. In 1958 a writer in the Evening Herald recalled that you could still ask at Dolphin’s Barn for the Back of the Pipes and be sent to the lone footpath to the canal bank behind St Kevin’s Hospital, and remembered the iron hand pumps in old city basements that lifted the basin’s low-pressure water to the cisterns upstairs, if you could afford one, and a maid to work it. Source: Irish Times, 4 March 1879 and 27 November 2020 (Frank McNally); Evening Herald, 2 May 1958. Show The Back of the Pipes on the map →

The first City Basin, a reservoir filled from the watercourse, was made around 1670. Between 1682 and 1721 Dublin’s population roughly doubled, from about 60,000 to 120,000, and in 1721 a new basin was built off James’s Street, between where St James’s Hospital and the Guinness Storehouse are now. It could hold about three months’ supply and served 90 streets. It was later joined to the Grand Canal. In the 18th century it was a fashionable promenade, approached through an ornamental arch at the end of Basin Lane, with walks lined with lime and elm, garden seats, bands, concerts and fireworks. Next to the basin, the brewery at St James’s Gate had the right to the same water under Arthur Guinness’s lease of 1759, and fought the city for it in 1775: see the meander Guinness and St James’s Gate . The visitor Richard Twiss was less impressed in 1775: both the springs and the reservoir were dry while he was in Dublin, and of the canal begun from it in 1765 he wrote that “it bids fair for being completed in three or four centuries.” After the canal line closed in 1974 the basin and harbour were filled in, but the names Basin View and Basin Street remain. In March 2023 Dublin City Council workers regenerating the linear park at Rialto, near the Fatima Luas stop, uncovered part of the old basin. Source: Betty Brunkard, Basin Street Harbour (Fountain Resource Group, 2014); The Journal, 16 March 2023. Show The City Basin on the map →

The water ended its journey at the Abbey of St Thomas the Martyr, off today’s Thomas Street. Henry II founded it in 1177 in atonement for the murder of Thomas Becket, and it was the only royal foundation in medieval Ireland. Its liberty, Thomas Court and Donore, controlled the western approach to the walled city, and it grew rich on lands in Meath, Dublin and Wicklow. Henry VIII dissolved it in the 1530s and gave it to William Brabazon, whose family became the Earls of Meath; the Earl of Meath’s Liberty lasted into the 19th century and gave the Liberties their name. Nothing of the abbey stands, but excavations on South Earl Street have found its remains. Show St Thomas’s Abbey on the map →

Meander · off Stop 14, St Patrick’s Cathedral Guinness and St James’s Gate Where Guinness got its water: not the Liffey but the Poddle, diverted by the monks in 1245 into the City Watercourse by a stone boat. Plus how Arthur Guinness defended that water with a pickaxe in 1775.
Where did Guinness get its water?

Not from the Liffey, as people often say, but from the Poddle, which was diverted by the monks of St Thomas’s Abbey in 1245 into the City Watercourse by a stone boat. The Stone Boat , just east of Sundrive Road in Kimmage, is a stone shaped like the bow of a boat, set in the river where the water brought from the Dodder at Balrothery joins the Poddle. It splits the flow two to one: two thirds stay in the Poddle, and one third goes off into the City Watercourse, an artificial channel that runs north to Dolphin’s Barn and then east along James’s Street to the city. It was rebuilt in 1555, and the stone there today is a modern replacement on the same design. Arthur Guinness’s lease of 1759 gave him that water free, as the next section shows. St James’s Gate was the western gate of the medieval city, on the road out past St Thomas’s Abbey. The City Watercourse, topped up from the Dodder, came in from Dolphin’s Barn along the Back of the Pipes, and a public cistern outside the gate is recorded from the 13th century. From 1721 the water was stored in the new City Basin off James’s Street, a few minutes’ walk south-west of the gate. For the brewers, maltsters and distillers along James’s Street and Thomas Street that water was everything: the Liffey was tidal and fouled, and could not be used for brewing. Source: D. McEntee and M. Corcoran, The Rivers Dodder and Poddle; Betty Brunkard, Basin Street Harbour (2014); Come Here To Me (2015).

On 31 December 1759 Arthur Guinness, then 34, took a lease of a small, disused brewery at St James’s Gate from Mark Rainsford, for 9,000 years at £45 a year. The Guinness Archive has shared the clause about the water. It gave him: “free use Liberty and privilidge of the said Pipe water or City Water Course Lying on the west of the premisses gratis and without any Consideration to be paid for the same as held and Enjoyed by the said Sir Mark Ransford for Brewing and Malting” , and the right to bring “Horses Carts Drays and Carriages” through the back way from Ransford Street. So the first Guinness was brewed with water that had come down the City Watercourse from the Poddle and the Dodder, past Templeogue, Kimmage and Dolphin’s Barn. Source: lease of 31 December 1759, extract courtesy of the Guinness Archive, Diageo Ireland.

Free water did not stay free for long. In 1772 a Corporation committee found two oversized pipes taking water into the brewery, and the city claimed Guinness was using far more than his lease allowed. On 16 May 1775 the committee came with the Sheriff and a gang of workmen to fill in the channel from the watercourse. Guinness, the committee reported, seized a pickaxe from one of the labourers, said that if they filled it up from end to end he would open it again at once, and that “the water was his, and he would defend it by force of arms”. The committee withdrew. The dispute ran on for almost ten years. It ended in a compromise: by one account on 24 May 1784, by another in 1785, Guinness agreed to take a lease of the water for the rest of his 9,000 years, at £10 a year. Source: Come Here To Me, “Arthur Guinness and his Right2Water” (2015), quoting the Dublin Historical Record (1947). Show St James’s Gate brewery on the map →
The Guinness family by the Poddle

The family left its mark downstream too, on the island between the two streams of the Poddle. Arthur’s grandson, Sir Benjamin Lee Guinness, paid for the restoration of St Patrick’s Cathedral from 1860 to 1865, when it was feared it might collapse. His son Edward Cecil Guinness, Lord Iveagh, cleared the slums of the “Poddle valley” north of the cathedral, where houses were sinking into the river, and laid out St Patrick’s Park, opened in 1902. His Iveagh Trust built the Bull Alley flats between 1901 and 1906, then the Iveagh Hostel and Iveagh Baths on Bride Road and, in 1915, the Iveagh Play Centre facing the cathedral. To give the new buildings firm ground the Corporation moved part of the Poddle’s course, with £1,400 from Lord Iveagh towards the new channel. Many brewery families lived along the river’s course. Around Blackpitts, many of Mary Agnes Hammond’s tenants were Guinness workers, and their deeds carried the right to wash in the River Poddle . Source: The Iveagh Trust, “The Vision for Bull Alley”; Dublin Corporation minutes, 1902.

The brewery even had a hand in the river’s first film. In the spring of 1968 Mike Lawlor of the Brewers’ Laboratory, chairman of the Guinness Film Society, gathered a few colleagues to make films as well as show them. Their first, a 27-minute colour film following a small sailing boat down the Liffey from its source in Wicklow to the Port of Dublin, was finished by early 1969 and a copy went to RTÉ; John Gleeson, also of the Brewers’ Laboratory, was one of the group. In November 1970 the brewery’s staff newsletter said the group’s next project, then being scripted, was “a definitive work on ‘The Liberties’”, to record what remained of “this unique area of Dublin”, and by 1972 Gleeson had been down the Barrow navigation by boat with a camera. That summer he was filming the City Watercourse between Firhouse and Kimmage, with narration by Sister Ann Dominica Fitzgerald . The Guinness Archive tells us the Film Society gave its films to the Irish Film Institute, so if the watercourse film, or the Liberties one, survives it should be there. The search goes on. Source: Evening Herald, 25 July 1972; The Harp (Guinness staff magazine), Autumn 1968, Spring 1969 and Spring 1972, and St James’s Gate newsletters, March 1969 and November 1970, courtesy of the Guinness Archive, Diageo Ireland. Meander · off Stop 11, Mount Jerome Along the Abbey Stream The monks’ mill stream, from the Hospice under the canal to Donore Avenue, Mill Street and Marrowbone Lane.

Near the gates of Mount Jerome the Poddle divides. The main river runs close to Harold’s Cross Road, and the second channel, the Abbey Stream, was a mill race that ran through the cemetery and into a mill pond at the far end of the hospice grounds. Both have long been culverted, and none of the river can be seen at the hospice today. In 1845 Mary Aikenhead, who founded the Religious Sisters of Charity in 1815 and St Vincent’s Hospital in 1834, bought Greenmount at Harold’s Cross and named it Our Lady’s Mount. It became the congregation’s mother house, with a night school, Sunday school and day school. After smallpox spread among the Sisters in 1879 they moved to Milltown, and the hospice for the incurable and dying that they had long planned opened at Harold’s Cross in the years that followed. In later years city councillors objected to plans to culvert more of the river through the hospice grounds. Show Our Lady’s Hospice on the map →

The river ran on from the hospice through what is now the Greenmount industrial estate, to a large mill pond. A corn mill here was turned into a cotton mill by James Greenham by 1807, the Greenmount Spinning Manufactory. In the mid-19th century the Quaker Pim family, of Pim Brothers on William Street, enlarged it into the Greenmount Spinning Company, making cotton, linen and the Irish poplin the family was known for; Frederic Pim later ran it. Its polychrome brick building, granite stairs and timber floors still stand. The mill pond was later used by bottling works, and was covered over in the late 1960s when the river to the canal was culverted, a change blamed for floods in the 1970s. Show Greenmount on the map →

North of the canal the Abbey Stream ran into the grounds of the Richmond Bridewell, a prison built for about £40,000 on the site of Grimwood’s nursery and used from 1813 to 1877. It held minor offenders in two walled quadrangles, with solitary confinement and flogging. The Fenian Joseph Poole was hanged there, and is thought to have been buried under what is now the boxing stadium. The War Department took the site in 1877, and it became Griffith Barracks; Griffith College is there now. The National Stadium opened in 1939 over the river. The Poddle added to its cost and delayed it, but the bowl-shaped hall seated 2,600, and boxing clubs paid 15 per cent of their takings towards the debt. Show The National Boxing Stadium on the map →

Donore Avenue, once Love Lane, runs from Cork Street to the South Circular Road and Parnell Bridge on the canal. The Abbey Stream came down it to meet the Tenter Water near the entrance to St Teresa’s Gardens, then turned at Brown Street towards the Coombe. Rev. Myles Ronan traced the abbey’s mill stream from Harold’s Cross to Donore Avenue and round by Pimlico, Ardee Street and Warrenmount, rejoining the old course of the Poddle, and dated it to between 1245 and 1324. When the abbey was dissolved in 1540 the stream drove four watermills: the Wattle Mill, the Wood Mill and the Double Mills. After the Reformation it was known as the Earl of Meath’s Watercourse. When the foundation stone of the new national schools on Donore Avenue was laid, the rector, the Rev. Fergus Greer, called the open river a drawback, and the Lord Mayor promised the Corporation would deal with it. In November 1902 the Local Government Board approved a loan of £450 for covering the river at Donore Avenue. In 1938 the Corporation diverted another stretch to build St Teresa’s Gardens. A footbridge over the stream could be seen until recently, and the river is still visible in the Greenville industrial estate. Show Donore Avenue on the map →

At the southern corner of Mill Street, by Sweeney’s Terrace, about 30 yards of the Poddle came up into the open. In the 1970s William Talbot, a local man descended from Huguenot weavers, showed reporters where it had been used for tanning, and kept timber from the old tanning tanks. The stream here fed the Double Mill of St Thomas’s Abbey, which made oil and flour. Local people had always known it: children played and fished in the mill race behind 6 Sweeney’s Terrace, and a man was said to have drowned there. In 1973 Sister Ann Dominica Fitzgerald led walks along the Poddle for the Dublin Arts Festival from Mount Argus to Warrenmount; by then the mill pond beside it had been cemented over. A student housing block on Mill Street was later required to keep part of the river visible, and an old millstone is on display. Mill Street is first named in 1711, in the will of Isaac Vauteau, a Huguenot whose descendants were tanners here. On 22 June 1875 fire broke out in the bonded stores off Cork Street. Whiskey from 5,000 burning hogsheads ran down Chamber Street, Ardee Street and Mill Street; people scooped it up in anything they had, even their boots, and several died from drinking it. Where the Poddle ran under Ardee Street the spirit ignited and the river exploded. Show Sweeney’s Terrace and Mill Street on the map →

Cork Street runs from the Coombe to Donore Avenue on the line of the old road west, the Slighe Dála, and is named after the first Earl of Cork. The Abbey Stream crosses it twice, near Emerald Square coming from the Coombe Hospital and again at Ardee Street on its way to Sweeney’s Terrace; the Commons Water runs behind the buildings on the north side; and the City Watercourse crossed it near the old ice rink on its way to the Back of the Pipes. You cannot see any of them now. It was a street of weavers. In 1815 Thomas Pleasants built the Tenter House here, a heated hall where weavers could stretch their cloth out of the weather. The Cork Street Fever Hospital opened in 1804 to fight typhus, was enlarged in 1817 to 1819, and later became the Brú Chaoimhín nursing home, which closed in 2011. The slender chimney behind the old Court furniture works belonged to J. and T. Ord’s tannery, later the Eustace Brothers’ dye works; deep vats and ox skulls were found during renovation. The 1925 relief works also turned a watercourse at Cork Street and Vauxhall into a sewer, at a cost of £2,000, to stop it flooding. Show Cork Street on the map →

Marrowbone Lane, off Cork Street, probably took its name from Marylebone in London, brought by London wool workers after 1690; Brooking’s map of 1728 has a version of the name, and by 1743 it was Marrowbone Lane. The City Watercourse, the Abbey Stream and the Commons Water all pass under or close to it, between Robert Street and Price’s Row. Huguenot, Dutch and Flemish weavers lived here in gabled “Dutch Billy” houses, a few of which survived into the 1980s. In 1916 Éamonn Ceannt’s men held the distillery here as an outpost of the South Dublin Union, and in the late 1930s Herbert Simms designed the curved flats that still follow the line of the street. Robert Collis’s play Marrowbone Lane (1939), staged by Hilton Edwards and Micheál Mac Liammóir, told of tenement life here. The river ran beneath the yards. Early in the 20th century Catherine Duffy was drawing water through a wooden trap in her courtyard when she lost her balance and fell into the swollen Poddle. Her neighbours watched her swept away into the dark; the street was dug up along the river, but her body was never found. Show Marrowbone Lane on the map →

Meander · off Stop 13, Cross Poddle The Liberties The old manors outside the walls, their weavers and the Poddle Guard.

The Liberties take their name from the manors outside the city walls that kept their own courts after the Normans came: the archbishop’s Liberty of St Sepulchre, and the Liberty of Thomas Court and Donore belonging to St Thomas’s Abbey. Between them they ran from the Liffey to St Patrick’s. Huguenot weavers made the area famous for cloth in the 17th and 18th centuries, but trade laws and changing markets brought decline, and by the 19th century it was a place of tenements. The Poddle and its branches run all through it. The main river comes from Blackpitts behind New Row and Clanbrassil Street, through Cross Poddle and down Patrick Street. The City Watercourse ran down the middle of Thomas Street from James’s Street towards Christ Church. The Commons Water runs behind Cork Street and the Coombe to St Patrick’s, and the Abbey Stream through Marrowbone Lane, Ardee Street and Mill Street.
The Poddle Guard and the City Sword

The Liberties kept their own peace, with the help of the Poddle Guard. On 4 August 1752, when the Lord Mayor and city officials rode the bounds of the Liberties, some mischief-makers at the Poddle snatched the ceremonial City Sword. The Poddle Guard caught the thief, who was sent to Newgate. In the same year, when the Liberty Boys heard that English cloth was being got ready for sale in Chamber Street and Weaver’s Square, they turned out in force and took more than ten pieces, burning or tearing five or six before the Poddle Guard broke them up. According to Rev. Myles Ronan, the Dodder and Poddle together brought the old city an average of 613,200 gallons a day, and after turning the mills the water served the dyers of the Liberties. Weaver’s Square and Ormond Street, off Cork Street, recall the Huguenot weavers who came in large numbers in the late 1600s at the invitation of the Duke of Ormond. Newmarket, laid out by the Earl of Meath in the 1670s, was their trading place. Weaving here is much older: digs in the Liberties have found Hiberno-Norse spindle whorls, weights and bone needles. The Weavers’ Hall on the Coombe, with its statue of George II holding the tools of the trade, is long gone, but its picture is kept in Dublin City Library and Archive. When the trade declined, the weavers turned to upholstery, lace and later motoring scarves and bow ties. The river did not run through the square, but its water did. In the early 1970s Corporation workmen laying new pipes found seven feet of oak water pipe, about seven inches across and with steel joints, five feet down. Thought to be about 250 years old, they were larger than any found in the city before. The workmen were Tommy Conway, John Burke, Peter Foran and Paddy Dunne. Show Weaver’s Square on the map →

Crosstick Alley, in the Liberty of St Thomas, ran from Francis Street to Meath Street. A 1971 article suggested its name came from a forgotten shrine or a crossing on the Poddle, but no map shows the river anywhere near it. Show Crosstick Alley on the map →

Meander · off Stop 15, Ship Street Little Christ Church Cathedral The cathedral on the ridge above the river, where St Patrick’s came when it flooded.

Christ Church stands on the ridge above the Poddle and the Liffey, at the end of Lord Edward Street. It was founded around 1028, after the Norse king Sitric Silkenbeard went on pilgrimage to Rome, with Dúnán as its first bishop. Henry II heard Mass here at Christmas 1171. It was rebuilt in stone from the 1180s, and its nave in the 1230s. In 1487 a pretender, Lambert Simnel, was crowned here, and in 1551 the service was sung in English for the first time in Ireland. George Edmund Street rebuilt much of it between 1871 and 1878, paid for by the distiller Henry Roe, and joined it by his covered bridge to the new Synod Hall, which takes in the tower of the old church of St Michael. The road schemes and the loss of the old houses at Wood Quay left it standing on its own. St Patrick’s, down by the river, often flooded, and in 1744 its chapter had to ask to hold their Lenten services at Christ Church, because their own cathedral was “dangerous to assemble in from the late floods”. Christ Church had its own water trouble in April 1953, when water was seeping into the basement of the Synod Hall. A water diviner found water 21 feet under High Street, though workmen digging 18 feet under the hall found none. Some blamed the Poddle; others a spring that had come back to life. Meander · off Stop 17, Palace Street St Andrew’s and Grafton Street A church that began in the fields by the Poddle, and a street closed for a river it never touched.

St Andrew’s church first stood in the fields near the Poddle, outside the walls; one writer imagines a pilgrim crossing a wooden bridge over the river on the way to it from St Mary del Dam. In 1670 it moved to St Andrew Street, to a site that had been a bowling green called Tib and Tom. The round church built there in 1793 to 1807 to designs by Francis Johnston burned in 1860, and Lanyon, Lynn and Lanyon’s church replaced it in 1862. The parish was one of those that paid the Poddle Tax in 1829. Show St Andrew’s on the map →

The Poddle never ran under Grafton Street; the Stein, another of Dublin’s hidden rivers, runs nearby. Even so, from 24 January 1988 the stretch between Chatham Street and South Anne Street was closed to traffic for about three weeks “to facilitate culverting of the Poddle River at Kimmage”, a notice that is still a puzzle. Stop 1 of 18 · Tallaght Fettercairn House Where the catchment begins, in the townland of Whitehall. In brief The Poddle’s catchment begins around Fettercairn House in Tallaght. From the hills above, the river runs about 11.6 km to the Liffey.

Fettercairn House (renamed St Mark’s House in 1985) appears on the first Ordnance Survey map of Ireland, printed in 1837. The house stands in the townland of Whitehall in Tamhlacht (Tallaght). It marks the southern edge of the Poddle catchment, where the stream is known as the Tymon Stream.
The Greater Dublin Strategic Drainage Study (2005) mapped the Poddle catchment beginning near Fettercairn House in Tallaght and stretching north-east through the city to the Liffey.

The environmental impact report for the flood scheme says the Poddle rises in the Cookstown area, north of Tallaght village. It flows east through Tymon North, the part of Tymon Park west of the M50, and then under the motorway into the main park. The report gives the river’s length as about 11.6 km and its catchment as about 16.4 square kilometres. It calls the Poddle a highly urbanised catchment, especially in the middle and lower reaches, where the river is culverted and channelled in sections.

The Poddle rises from a spring, now underground, opposite St Mark’s School in Cookstown, close to Fettercairn House. At its source it is called the Tymon River. Nothing marks the spot. Its first course ran east through what is now Cookstown Industrial Estate, but building has rerouted it and put it in pipes as far as the Belgard Road. The first open water you can see is behind the Trulife factory on Airton Road, along the northern edge of the TU Dublin Tallaght campus. From there the river runs east to the Gallagher factory, turns south to the Greenhills Road and passes under it, then flows east through Bancroft Park, under the Castletymon Road and through the grounds of Tallaght Community School before it turns north into Tymon Park. Stop 2 of 18 · Tallaght Bancroft The first stretch of the river you can walk beside. In brief Bancroft Park is the first public stretch of the Poddle, named after a castle that has long since gone.

The name Bancroft comes from the castle that once stood at the present junction of Greenhills Road and Tallaght Village. The castle’s history is uncertain, but its lands formed part of the wider Tymon estate.
Bancroft Park, a northern extension of Tymon Park, is the first publicly accessible section of the Poddle. Upstream of here, the channel runs through the grounds of Technological University Dublin.

A short walk away, just off Tallaght’s main street by the old walls of St Mary’s Dominican Priory, a plaque put up by Tallaght Community Council in 2022 marks a spot called Talbot’s Leap. It is a reminder that water shaped Tallaght village too. In the 1600s, the plaque says, a drawbridge stood here over a stream that carried water to the Archbishop of Dublin’s bathhouse. The archbishops had a castle and later a palace at Tallaght; the priory now stands on its site and keeps its old tower. The stream now runs through Sean Walsh Park, but its old stone channel can still be seen running under the priory wall, and the site of the bathhouse is to the front left of the Dominican church. The story goes back to the Cromwellian wars. The Talbots of Belgard Castle, a branch of the great Norman family that also held Malahide, were Catholic royalists who fought against Cromwell; Belgard was ruined in the war and John Talbot followed Charles II into exile. Around 1651, the plaque says, Cromwell’s soldiers raided and plundered Belgard. Talbot gathered his best men, chased them and caught up with them at Tallaght, but the Ironsides were too strong. Retreating, he found the drawbridge raised, and he and his men jumped their horses across the watercourse to escape. William Handcock, writing in the 1870s, tells the same tradition and places the leap “where the little stream now crosses the road, as you go up to the church”. This is local tradition, not recorded history. Cromwell himself is not known to have come to Tallaght, though his soldiers certainly did: in 1651 a Captain Alland was quartered there, stripped the roof, timber and pews from St Maelruain’s church for his own buildings, and, so the story goes, fed his horses from the church’s stone font. The parish was paid £100 in compensation in 1662. The Talbots survived the Commonwealth. After the Restoration John Talbot recovered at least part of the Belgard estate and rebuilt the castle. He fought for James II at the Boyne, Aughrim and Limerick, was covered by the Articles of Limerick, and retired to Belgard. He had no son, and through his daughter Catherine’s marriage the house passed to the Dillons. Colonel John Talbot of Belgard is buried in St Maelruain’s churchyard; accounts differ on whether he was a captain or a colonel, and on the year he died.

The heritage chapter of the flood scheme’s environmental report says that stray prehistoric finds from the Bancroft and Dodder river areas of Tallaght village point to early occupation. Two bronze artefacts, found in 1973, came from Bancroft Grove, about 250 m south of Tymon Park. The same chapter records that nothing of archaeological significance was found when Bancroft Park was monitored in 2003, and that no recorded prehistoric sites lie within the area of the scheme itself.

Stop 3 of 18 · Tymon Park Tymon A ruined castle, a glacial esker and the park built around them. In brief A ruined tower house, an Ice Age esker and now the flood lake: Tymon Park holds the river’s past and is the most accessible part of the watercourse today.

The castle is thought to have been built in either the 12th or the 15th century, as a defensive outpost against Irish clans raiding the Pale. By 1547 it was recorded as ruinous, and it seems to have stayed that way, uninhabited for most of its life. During the 1798 rebellion, the body of a rebel was left at the castle by his comrades after they were attacked by soldiers near Oldbawn. British soldiers then hung it from the doorway and left it there. The Poddle flowed through the marshy ground below, with the castle on the higher ground of the esker.

In 1216 King John granted the manor of Timothan to Henry de Loundres (Henry of London), Archbishop of Dublin, and his successors, said to be in recompense for his losses in fortifying Dublin Castle. Ownership later passed through many hands, including William Conolly (1662–1729), Speaker of the Irish House of Commons. The lands later had a complex mix of owners and uses, including quarrying and farming. The state acquired them in the 1970s and opened them as a public park in 1980.

Tymon Park now does a new job for the river. Under the River Poddle Flood Alleviation Scheme, the eastern end of the lake embankment has been raised and the old weir replaced by a flow-control structure. In a big storm, the lake at Limekiln can now rise by up to three metres, holding water back until the peak has passed downstream. The impoundment came into use on 20 February 2025, the first part of the scheme to be finished.

Tymon Esker, along which Tymon Lane now runs, is a rare and important feature of the park. An esker is a long ridge of sand and gravel laid down by a stream flowing under a glacier, in this case during the last Ice Age, more than 10,000 years ago. Tymon Lane, along the ridge, was an important link between Tallaght and the townlands of Dublin, and Tymon Castle was built beside it.

Greenhills was mostly farmland until the 1950s and 1960s, when the housing estates were built. The Greenhills Road runs from Tallaght village to the Walkinstown Roundabout, and the Poddle passes under it near St Mary’s Priory before it enters Tymon Park. The wider Greenhills area takes in part of Tymon and runs east as far as Templeville Road. Show Greenhills on the map →

The lands for Tymon Park were bought by compulsory purchase in the 1970s. They had been farmed, some by the same families for a hundred years or more. The park covers about 130 hectares between Tallaght, Templeogue and Walkinstown and opened to the public in June 1986. The M50 later split it in two, and footbridges near the Greenhills Road and the Tallaght–Templeogue road join the halves. In the western park the Poddle first follows its old line beside Tymon Lane, then turns into a new course of ponds, cascades and waterfalls made in the 1980s. The western lakes were dug in 1985, one of them in an old quarry. About 50,000 cubic metres of soil were moved to shape the banks and viewing mounds. Four ponds are linked by sluices, cascades and underground channels, and a dense clay called marl in the ground holds the water without a liner. Within two years mallard were nesting. In 1997 three more lakes, covering 2.2 hectares, were dug in the eastern park near Limekiln Road. They were paid for partly by the developer of new housing at Kimmage Manor, which was required to reduce the flood risk downstream, and they were built to hold at least 13,000 cubic metres of flood water. Four football pitches went, more than 100,000 cubic metres of earth were moved, and islands were left in the lakes for water birds. Source: South Dublin County Council, a book on the facilities and history of Tymon Park (2001), South Dublin Libraries hdl.handle.net/10599/8965 .

Tymon Castle was a two-storey tower on the ridge beside Tymon Lane, with a vaulted ceiling, a flat roof, a projecting stair turret and machicolations, the overhanging parapets from which defenders could drop missiles on attackers. It was described as ruinous by 1547. In the 1770s it was partly repaired and briefly lived in by a poor family, and for generations it was a place for picnics. By the 20th century it was a dangerous ruin, and it was knocked down in 1960. Local tradition says the castle was built to guard the river’s source. Show Tymon Park on the map →

Stop 4 of 18 · Firhouse, on the Dodder Balrothery Weir Where medieval engineers turned the Dodder towards the city. In brief Medieval monks turned part of the Dodder towards Dublin here before 1244, and the Poddle has been part of the Dodder’s story ever since.

Balrothery Weir, also called Firhouse Weir, the City Weir or the Great Weir, sits on the Dodder in the Dodder Valley Park, close to where the M50 crosses the river. For more than 500 years it mattered to every citizen of Dublin, because most of the water they drank came over it. Here the Dodder was turned out of its own bed and sent north-east in a man-made channel, the first stretch of the City Watercourse. About three kilometres on, that channel met the stream coming down from Tallaght, and from that meeting the river is the Poddle proper. Everything downstream, the Tongue, the mills of Kimmage and Harold’s Cross, the cisterns at James’s Street and the moat of Dublin Castle, depended on this weir. The names are argued over. Firhouse is the village on the south bank and Balrothery the townland on the north bank, where the watercourse began. Older writers also spell it Balruddery. In 2021 a South Dublin County Council motion to rename it officially as Firhouse Weir was voted down, and the Record of Protected Structures lists it as “City Watercourse, Firhouse”.

The Poddle is a small river with a small catchment, and in a dry summer it carried very little. By the early 13th century it had to supply St Thomas’s Abbey, the tenants of the cathedrals and a fast-growing Norman city, and it could not. The Dodder was the obvious answer. It rises on Kippure, in the Wicklow Mountains, and runs about 29 kilometres to Ringsend, fast and well fed by mountain rain. At Firhouse it passes within three kilometres of the Poddle, and on higher ground, so water taken off here could run downhill all the way to the city.

The usual story is that the canons of St Thomas’s Abbey built the weir before 1244, to feed their mills and their own water supply, and that the citizens enlarged it in 1244. The sources do not agree on the dates, and we give them here side by side. The firmest date is a writ of 29 April 1244. The justiciar, Maurice Fitzgerald, ordered the sheriff of Dublin to hold an inquiry “by twelve free and lawful men” into “whence water can be best and most conveniently taken from its course and conducted to the King’s city of Dublin”, at the citizens’ cost, and to report any damage it might do. The Dodder weir was chosen, and enlarged and repaired. In 1245 the King told John FitzGeffrey to finish his hall in Dublin Castle and to have water piped to it by the summer of 1246, which suggests the works were done by then. Other writers give other dates. H. F. Berry (1891) puts the watercourse in the middle of the 13th century and wrote about an inquisition of 1258, which recent reports date to 1259, recording an agreement between the monks and the citizens. Rev. Myles Ronan (1927) says the watercourse was formed between 1245 and 1254. B. Mac Giolla Phádraig (1954) dates the weir to 1254. Simpson (1997), as summarised in the flood scheme’s heritage report, reads the evidence the other way: the monks had already diverted the Dodder at Firhouse, the 1244 works were the second branch at Harold’s Cross, and the weir could date from as early as the late 12th century.

A weir is a low wall across a river that raises the water behind it. At Firhouse the wall runs diagonally across the Dodder, which makes it longer and lets it hold up a wide, calm pool. On the north bank, at the head of that pool, a set of sluice gates opened into the City Watercourse. Raise the gates and water ran off into the channel; close them and the river carried on over the weir. In normal weather nearly the whole river was turned into the watercourse. Writing in the 1870s, William Handcock said that except in floods “the whole river” went that way, and only the flood water went on down the old bed. Ronan reckoned that the city took an average of about 613,200 gallons a day, roughly 2.8 million litres, and that the Abbey mills took twice that. From the sluices the channel ran across the fields, under the Tallaght road, past the old churchyard at Templeogue and through the grounds of Templeogue House, joining the Tallaght stream about a quarter of a mile north of Mount Down, near Whitehall. Mills crowded along it. In 1844 Robert Mallet counted 24 mills at work on the Dodder, 12 of them on the City Watercourse.

A supply this long, running through private land, was easy to tamper with. The city appointed keepers for the stretch from the Dodder to the Tongue, usually a yeoman living near Tallaght or Templeogue: John Pylle of Templeogue in 1456 and a Walsh in 1491. Millers and landowners still cut holes in the banks to take more than their share. Sometimes the water was cut off on purpose. Rebels following Silken Thomas broke the supply in 1534. The Talbots of Templeogue, through whose land it ran, blocked it in a quarrel with the mill owners; Weston St John Joyce dates this to 1573 and again 1689, other accounts to 1597. In the wars of the 1640s royalist forces are said to have cut it to leave the Cromwellian garrison in Dublin short of water and milling. The most famous threat is a story about the Hellfire Club. In August 1738 Henry Barry, Lord Santry, ran a tavern porter, Laughlin Murphy, through with his sword in Palmerstown. He was tried by his fellow peers in 1739 and sentenced to death. His uncle, Sir Compton Domvile of Templeogue House, is said to have let it be known that he would turn off the city’s water where it crossed his land. Santry was reprieved and given a full pardon in 1740, and died in England in 1751. The threat is told by many writers but is best treated as legend; Joyce even says the authorities helped Santry escape, which does not match the record of the pardon. By 1718 the water arriving in the city was badly fouled, and an inquiry traced the pollution to a paper mill and a tuck mill. The result was the 1719 Act “for cleansing and repairing the watercourse from the River Dodder to the City of Dublin”, which gave the Corporation much stronger powers over the whole channel.

What you see today is not medieval. In 1308 the mayor, John Le Decer, had the watercourse cleaned and its banks faced with stone, though it is not recorded whether he worked on the weir itself. The National Inventory of Architectural Heritage dates the present weir to about 1775, and says it is about 80 metres long and drops in three main stages from the weir pool to the river, with a group of sluice gates at the weir and nearby. Later accounts describe a final modernisation of the weir and sluices in the early 19th century, and an archaeologist in 2001 judged it largely remodelled in Victorian times. That 2001 work, monitoring the removal of gravel above the weir for flood relief and the linear park, found masonry walls along the south bank and eight hollowed-out tree trunks in the riverbed. They were probably water pipes, like the 18th-century wooden pipes found under Dublin’s streets. Nothing older was found, and the report notes that the weir was quarried for river gravel until the 19th century.

Before the river was straightened and deepened in the 1840s you could drive across just below the weir. Afterwards the banks stood about 20 feet high, and the only way over in a flood was to wade along the top of the weir, which Handcock called dangerous. A wooden footbridge paid for by local subscription was swept away in a flood, and its planks were said to have floated down to Ringsend. An iron lattice bridge followed around 1860, 20 feet above the riverbed. The present bridge was opened by South Dublin County Council in 1995.

The weir’s job faded slowly. The Grand Canal began to supply the city basin in the 18th century; the flood scheme’s heritage report gives 1755, and Berry, quoted by Handcock, says the city relied on the Dodder until 1775. In the 19th century the Vartry and Bohernabreena reservoirs took over the drinking supply, and the watercourse was kept for mills and industry. Even in 1939 J. Hegarty could describe “the weir, the watercourse, the Tongue” as still in place and still doing some of their old work. In the middle of the 20th century parts of the channel were piped. In the 1970s new housing at Templeogue and Firhouse cut through its line, and newspaper letters at the time warned that bad planning would bury it. The link from the Dodder to the Poddle was then allowed to dry out. Today only a short stub of channel leaves the weir and ends within about 100 metres.

The weir is in the Dodder Valley Park, between Firhouse and Balrothery, beside the M50 bridge over the Dodder. You can walk to it along the riverside path from Old Bawn or from Firhouse, both of which have parking. Stand on the 1995 footbridge for the best view of the falls, then look to the north bank for the old sluices and the start of the dry channel. It is a protected structure, and the National Inventory rates it of regional importance for its archaeological, architectural and technical interest. From the weir, a path under the M50 takes you into Tymon Park and on to the Poddle itself. The Dodder rises fast after heavy rain. Keep to the paths and the bridge, and do not try to cross on the weir.

People in Firhouse tend to call it Firhouse Weir and people in Tallaght Balrothery Weir. In 2021 a motion at South Dublin County Council to rename it officially as Firhouse Weir was voted down, and the Record of Protected Structures still lists it as “City Watercourse, Firhouse”. It is also recorded as a historic engineering work. Show What’s in a name on the map →

From the weir the City Watercourse ran across the fields, under the Tallaght road and through the grounds of Templeogue House before turning north to meet the Tymon River. Whoever held Templeogue held the city’s water. In the 14th century the lands belonged to the Harold family, and by the 16th century to the Talbots, who held them for about 200 years. The owner kept the watercourse in repair and was paid in corn by the mills that used the water. In 1655 there was a castle, a tuck mill, a house and cottages, with about 40 people. In 1686 the lands were mortgaged to Sir Thomas Domville for £3,000, and after Sir James Talbot was attainted in 1688 for supporting James II, Domville took them. He built a brick mansion on the site of the castle, keeping its vaulted undercroft and two round towers. His son, Sir Compton Domville, laid out the grounds around the watercourse, lining it up on the front door and sending it down a flight of steps decorated with statues, and built a circular temple on a mound in one of the fields. The Domvilles took the miller’s corn and rents from St Patrick’s Cathedral and the Earl of Meath, and they were not afraid to use their power over the water: see the story of Lord Santry above. After Sir Compton died in 1768 his nephew Charles Pocklington lived at Templeogue until about 1780, then moved to Santry, taking many of the ornaments, the temple among them. Around 1820 a Mr Gogerty rebuilt the house, again keeping the old undercroft and towers. The novelist Charles Lever lived there from 1842 to 1845. The dry channel of the watercourse still runs straight to the front door, lined with mature trees. In 1972 an archaeologist from the National Museum examined the temple mound to see whether it was an ancient burial mound; nothing ancient was found. Show Templeogue House on the map →

Stop 5 of 18 · Tymon Park M50 Crossing Where the motorway sent the river underground. In brief The river passes under the M50 here, in a culvert, where the motorway splits Tymon Park in two.

The M50 was planned in the 1970s, and building began in the 1980s with this section, from the N7 to the N81, first built as a single-carriageway road. The state’s purchase of the Tymon estate for the park was probably either a result of the road scheme or part of the same plan. The Poddle was presumably culverted at this point to carry it under the future motorway.
In 1990 the N3 to N81 section of the M50 opened, including the West Link bridge across the Liffey Valley, and this stretch was upgraded from single carriageway to motorway.

Tymon Park is split in two by the M50. The flood scheme’s documents call the part west of the motorway Tymon North and the part east of it Tymon Park. The Poddle flows through Tymon North, passes under the motorway and carries on into Tymon Park. East of the M50 a field inspection in March 2019 noted a number of ponds in the park, and that at the park’s eastern end the river runs behind the gardens of a housing estate.

Stop 6 of 18 · Lakelands, Terenure Dodder Overflow A sluice that sends flood water back to the Dodder. In brief A sluice and channel that send flood water from the Poddle back towards the Dodder at Terenure.

Upstream of Kimmage Manor, where the Poddle begins its first long run in culverts, the river divides twice. This is the first. Unlike the second, it sends high water out of the Poddle and into the Dodder catchment, by way of storage ponds in Terenure.

A sluice gate limits how much water carries on towards Kimmage and Kimmage Road Lower. The overflow runs through culverts to the ponds at Terenure College, which drain back to the Dodder at Bushy Park. An old record of the City Watercourse says a stream taken off it in Terenure fed three fishponds, so the idea of ponds there is an old one. You can follow the overflow on the map page, where it is drawn as a green dashed line from the point where it leaves the Poddle beside Whitehall Park to the lake in the grounds of Terenure College. The line is approximate, since the culverts are underground. This is the downstream end of the flow controls and channel works in the River Poddle Flood Alleviation Scheme. The scheme followed serious floods in Harold’s Cross and Kimmage in 1987, 1990, 1993 and 2011. It was approved by An Bord Pleanála in June 2023, the Office of Public Works began building it in April 2024, and it is due to be finished in 2027.

Along this stretch, the scheme proposes to tidy and define the channel and build walls on both sides. Flows through the Poddle in earlier centuries must have been large, without the ponds at Tymon or these control structures, and with water diverted in from the Dodder at Balrothery as well.
Mount Down: where the Poddle begins

Just east of Tymon Park the river runs behind the houses on Limekiln Road, under a bridge at Wellington Lane, and turns north towards Templeville Road. Near here, on land between today’s Glendown Grove and Wellington Lane, the City Watercourse from the Dodder met the Tymon River, and from that meeting the stream is the Poddle proper. Mount Down House and its mill stood beside the junction. The house had 47 acres beside Kimmage Manor and Orwell House. Its residents included Anna Danford (1886 to 1888), Anna and Sir Robert Herron (1888 to 1895), and Thomas Franks and John Kean (1895 to 1916). The Cullen family farmed there from 1916 to 1969, mostly dairy cattle, and lit the house with a generator driven by the two streams. The mill beside the house was not worked in their time. The house was knocked down in 1973 for the Glendown estate and St Mary’s Rugby Club; two chestnut trees from its avenue still stand in Glendown. In 1952 Peter Cullen sued Dublin Corporation for £20,000 and an injunction, claiming that the ancient water supply that had turned his mill since 1244 had been dwindling since 1938. He valued the property at £10,000 with the water and £7,000 without. The Corporation denied reducing the flow or that he had any right to it, and the claim was dismissed. Source: The Story of Templeogue (1992); newspaper reports, 1952. Show Mount Down: where the Poddle begins on the map →

On the eastern side of Tymon Park the river runs between the Willington and Osprey estates and Limekiln Road. The Willington name may come from nearby Wellington Lane. In 1954 this was the scene of a famous arrest. John Broe, a 30-year-old housebreaker the papers called “The Phantom”, had kept Dublin talking with a run of daring burglaries. Detective Officer Christopher Lang spotted him hiding under a haycock near Wellington Lane and chased him to the Poddle, where they fought for twenty minutes. Broe got away, but Gardaí John Egan and Walter Dowd soon found him in a ditch nearby. When the estates were built in the early 1970s, they went over the 700-year-old Dodder branch of the City Watercourse, and under the neighbouring Glendown estate the channel was put in a culvert. Historians objected at the time: a 1972 article warned that the watercourse at Wellington Lane faced destruction with no plan to preserve it, and Sister Ann Dominica Fitzgerald campaigned to save it. In 1978, only six years after the houses went up, storms flooded the new estates. The Poddle burst its banks at Templeogue and homes in Osprey Drive were flooded again and again; residents such as Peter and Kathleen Smith described struggling with each new flood. Councillor Seán Walsh blamed the drainage, especially a culvert at Wellington Lane too small for the run-off from the new estates. Residents felt the council had been slow to act, and said it was the State, not the developer, that paid into the emergency fund for repairs. Show Willington and Osprey on the map →

Stop 7 of 18 · Kimmage Kimmage Manor A Victorian MP’s house, now a mission centre, built over the stream. In brief A Victorian MP’s house, now a mission centre, built over the stream at Kimmage.

In 1641 the lands of Kimmage, Terenure and Milltown all belonged to Peter Barnewall, and there was a castle in good repair at Kimmage. Owners and tenants came and went. Rocque’s map from the mid-18th century shows extensive buildings where the Manor House stands today.

In 1829 Frederick Shaw and his family came to live at Kimmage, in an L-shaped part of the present manor facing today’s Mission House. Sir Frederick lived there until his death in 1876. A year after moving in, Shaw was elected MP for Dublin City, in 1830, and was re-elected in 1832. He then sat for Dublin University from 1832 to 1848, and became a Privy Councillor in 1835. He was regarded as one of the finest speakers and debaters in Parliament. One of his best-known speeches, in 1834, opposed Daniel O’Connell’s motion for a select committee into Baron Smith, who had been accused of bringing politics into his charge to a grand jury.

The river enters the grounds from the west and is then piped under later additions to the manor. The manor later became a house of the Holy Ghost Fathers, and then the Kimmage Mission Institute and Development Studies Centre. The upstream sluice keeps the flow here under control and limits the risk of flooding to the buildings, with most of the water sent around the north of the site.

Below Templeville Road the river flows north-east through the edge of Perrystown towards Kimmage Manor, running more or less parallel to Whitehall Road. It passes between the Wainsfort and Manor estates and behind Whitehall Gardens into the St Anne’s estate. Much of this stretch is still open, despite the housing built around it. The river was the boundary between Perrystown and Kimmage House. In 1905, in a fair rent case, Mary Ida Clayton, the tenant of Perrystown, argued that it was a separate farm and not part of Sir Frederick Shaw’s demesne at Kimmage. Her counsel pointed to the Poddle dividing the two, with three bridges over it. Show Perrystown on the map →
From Kimmage House to Kimmage Manor

The house stands in the townland of Kimmage, but its grounds cross the Poddle into Perrystown. It was “The House” of Frederick Shaw’s Crumlin estate, and he had the architects Richard and William Morrison remodel it in a Tudor revival style, with gables, spiral turrets and tall chimneys. Shaw also built a new approach, Whitehall Road, in place of the old avenue from the Kimmage side, which ran from about where Greenlea Road is now. The road’s Irish name, Bóthar an Racardáir, the Recorder’s Road, recalls his post as Recorder of Dublin. He is said to have voted with Peel to repeal the Corn Laws, against most of his party, and to have turned down the post of Lord Lieutenant. One of his granddaughters, Flora Shaw, proposed the name Nigeria in 1897 while she was colonial editor of The Times. Sir Frederick was buried in St Mary’s churchyard, Crumlin. After his death the house was let, to Erskine Chetwode among others, and in 1898 it was leased in perpetuity to William and Mary Ida Clayton. Only then was it called Kimmage Manor; the title was a name, not a manor in any legal sense. In 1911 the Holy Ghost Fathers, now the Spiritans, bought it as a training house for missionary priests, and it became their headquarters. Its church served Crumlin parish as a chapel of ease until it became a parish itself in 1990. Land was given for Templeogue College in the 1960s, and more was sold in the 1990s for the housing on Whitehall Road and Wainsfort Road. Source: T. McCarthy, The Shaws of Terenure (Four Courts Press, 2010); P. J. Ryan, Kimmage Manor: 100 Years of Service to the Mission (Columba Press, 2011). Show From Kimmage House to Kimmage Manor on the map →

Stop 8 of 18 · Kimmage Cross Roads Ravensdale and Poddle Park A valley of mills, and the scheme’s main flood storage in the city. In brief A valley of old mills, and now the scheme’s main flood storage within the city.

Between Kimmage Cross Roads and Sundrive Road the Poddle was once lined with mills. The first Ordnance Survey maps of the 1830s and 1840s show Ravensdale Mills, a corn and flour mill with its own pond, sluice and weir on Kimmage Road Lower, where Ravensdale Park is today. It was still marked on the map in 1940. Downstream, Larkfield Mills and its pond stood where Sundrive Shopping Centre is now, and another mill and pond sat beside the river near today’s St Martin’s Drive, with a windmill nearby on the same old mill-pond ground. The stump of a windmill survives in St Martin’s Park. At Larkfield, the Plunkett family’s mill and farm later served as a store for weapons landed in the Howth gun-running of 1914. Near the crossroads, Farrington’s flour mill ran a water turbine into the 1920s; Mr Farrington is remembered as the first person in the area with electric light, until the ESB arrived and he had to stop.

Past Kimmage Manor the river runs underground through St Anne’s, comes up near the crossroads, dives under the junction and emerges again in Ravensdale Park. It once flowed through the grounds of Brooklawn, a large house beside the crossroads, and through the St Anne’s estate, where its banks stood fifteen to twenty feet high. When developers proposed flats on the St Anne’s lands in the early 1970s, with the river to be culverted, the plans were opposed. Dublin Corporation and Dublin County Council refused one scheme for 108 flats on 10 January 1974, citing the river and the land’s zoning as open space.

This stretch is central to the River Poddle Flood Alleviation Scheme. Ravensdale Park is being reshaped to store flood water, with new flood walls and a replacement footbridge. Poddle Park gets walls, a sloped path and a new pedestrian bridge, and a flood wall is planned at the end of St Martin’s Drive. Behind Grosvenor Court the river is being realigned with embankments on both sides. Works began in Ravensdale Park in 2025.

The big houses around the crossroads are remembered by Finola Watchorn in Crumlin and the Way it Was. Kimmage Lodge, a large Georgian house behind today’s Glenanne apartments, was the home of the Davy family; the Rev. Humphrey Davy was rector of St Mary’s, Crumlin, from 1867 to 1913. Wainsfort and Fortfield Lodge stood on Fortfield Road, and Fortfield Lodge marked the edge of Kimmage, which ran from Harold’s Cross Green up to it. Her grandfather, P. J. Watchorn, built the KCR petrol station in the early 1930s. The Glenanne Sports Club, formed in 1943 from the Graftonians, played on the grounds of St Anne’s, a small estate running from the crossroads up to the back of Kimmage Manor. The Poddle ran through it between banks 15 to 20 feet high, which gave the place the look of a glen and the club its name. The club lost its grounds in 1970, when the land was sold for building. Ravensdale Mill, also called the Tinker flour mill, stood at the corner of Kimmage Road Lower and Captain’s Lane, now Captain’s Road, with its entrance on Captain’s Lane. Pat Johnson of the Old Dublin Society remembered its iron wheel, about eight feet across, turned by the Poddle, driving the mill’s three floors through gears and a vertical shaft; the millstone was still intact in 1928. The Drake family ran the mill and lived in a two-storey house nearby. Milling stopped around 1917. From 1924 Joe P. Kelly and his three sons made furniture there until the business failed in 1928. By the 1940s little was left. Finola Watchorn played in the ruins on the way home from school, and Lizzie Moran kept a small sweet shop in part of them. Source: Finola Watchorn, Crumlin and the Way it Was. Show Ravensdale Mill on the map →

Between Ravensdale Park and Bangor Road the river gives its name to the streets: Poddle Park, Poddle Green, Poddle View and Poddle Close. The Poddle Park cottages were built for labourers in the 1920s and 1930s, St Martin’s Park and Drive in the 1960s, the Riverside apartments in the 2000s on the site of Brennan’s bakery, Poddle Close on the back gardens of the Clonard Road cottages, and Poddle Green and Poddle View on the grounds of Waterpark House. In 1967 Dublin Corporation laid out St Martin’s on Martin’s Lands and realigned, deepened and regraded the river to cut flooding. The stretch from Ravensdale Park to Poddle Park was put in a culvert and the river was turned under the Poddle Park road. The stepping stones at the top of Bangor Road, a shortcut for hundreds of factory workers, gave way to a concrete and steel footbridge, which vandals wrecked in 1968. Local people have long looked after this stretch. In 1973 a city commissioner, George Butler, asked for action on rubbish dumped in the river at St Martin’s Drive and on oil pollution that kept appearing at weekends. In September 1974 the St Martin’s Residents’ Association and Dublin Corporation cleaned the river together, and the association drew up a ten-point plan: notices against dumping, a safe bridge at Bangor Road, an end to oil from local industry, and trees and flowers on the banks. The floods kept coming. In October 2002 Mary Byrne, then 84, spent the night with her family fighting 18 inches of water in her kitchen in Poddle Park, as she had in the 1986 storm. A new footbridge upstream of the old one was proposed in 2004, and the current flood scheme adds a 1.5-metre wall in Poddle Park. Show Poddle Park and St Martin’s on the map →

Stop 9 of 18 · Sundrive Road, Kimmage The Stone Boat The medieval stone that splits the river two to one. In brief A stone shaped like a boat’s bow splits the river at Kimmage, sending part of it to St Thomas’s Abbey.

Just east of Sundrive Road, a stone shaped like the bow of a boat divides the river. The first was built in 1245, when the Norman city of Dublin was short of water. It was rebuilt in 1555, and the stone you see today is a modern replacement on the same design. The canons of St Thomas’s Abbey carried out extensive works to bring water to their abbey and the city. These works took water from the Dodder at Balrothery to Kimmage, where it joined the Poddle. Here the stone tongue, known locally as the Stone Boat, split the flow two to one: two thirds stayed in the Poddle, and one third went into the City Watercourse.

The City Watercourse, an artificial channel, carried its third of the water north-west towards Dolphin’s Barn. Near today’s Basin Lane it turned east along the south side of James’s Street and through Thomas Street into the city. The Augustinian Abbey of St Thomas the Martyr lay outside the medieval walls, in the western suburbs just off modern Thomas Street. It was founded in 1177 by William FitzAldelm, custos of Ireland, on behalf of King Henry II, and followed the Victorine rule, like St Augustine’s Abbey in Bristol, so its first canons probably came from Bristol. No trace of the abbey survives.
Larkfield Mill and the Kimmage Garrison

Larkfield Mill stood where Sundrive Shopping Centre is now. In 1816 it was a skin mill; in the 1880s William Danford ran a corn mill there; later it was Larkfield Roller Mills, run by Harron, Connolly and Co.; and by the 1930s it housed St Kevin’s Paint Works. Before the 1916 Rising the lease was held by Countess Plunkett, wife of Count George Noble Plunkett: twenty acres, some cottages, a barn and the mill, by then idle. Her sons, among them Joseph Mary Plunkett, used it as a base. Arms from the Howth gun-running of 1914 passed through it, and in the months before the Rising about 90 Irish Volunteers who had come over from Britain lived and trained there, making munitions. They became known as the Kimmage Garrison. Patrick Pearse spoke to them the week before the Rising. Show Larkfield Mill and the Kimmage Garrison on the map →

The wedge-shaped stone that splits the river gave its name to the Tongue Fields and the Tonguefield housing around them, and in turn to the Stone Boat pub nearby. A newspaper correspondent once remembered a button factory in the Tongue Fields, driven by the river. Finola Watchorn traces the two branches from here. The artificial branch, with a third of the water, went north to Dolphin’s Barn and was carried on a raised bank, remembered as the Back of the Pipes, to the City Basin near James’s Street. The old course carried on through the grounds of Mount Argus and Loader’s Park Mills, along Kimmage Road Lower, under the front gardens of some of its houses, and down Harold’s Cross Road to the canal, then on by Clanbrassil Street, Blackpitts, New Row and Patrick Street.
