Stop 10 of 18 · Harold’s Cross Mount Argus Flood defences in a park, beside the church of a saint. In brief A park beside a historic monastery, where mills once stood.

Past the Stone Boat, most of the Poddle’s flow enters the grounds of Mount Argus. Here modern flood-control features sit in parkland, and this is the last easily reached stretch of the river before its long run underground begins. Dublin Corporation’s minutes for 1979 record the river at Mount Argus being included in an amenity improvement scheme.
Mount Argus, in Harold’s Cross, was the first Passionist monastery in Ireland, founded in 1856. The present church was built between 1873 and 1878 and dedicated to St Paul of the Cross in 1878.

In the monastery grounds the Poddle once fed a pond and a millrace. Harold’s Cross was then a small mill village: a paper mill worked at Mount Argus in the 19th century, and Loader’s Park Mills, a corn mill on Kimmage Road Lower, stood where the Waterwheel apartments are now. On Mount Argus Road a former flour mill later became a laundry, and is now apartments. The old Mount Argus mill, long disused, was taken over in the 20th century by the 45th Mount Argus Scout Troop as a boxing club.

Charles Houben arrived at the newly founded monastery on 9 July 1857. Known for his gift of healing, he drew as many as 300 people a day to Mount Argus to be blessed. He died there on 5 January 1893, aged 71. Hundreds of cures were credited to him in his lifetime and after. He was beatified by Pope John Paul II in 1988 and canonised by Pope Benedict XVI on 3 June 2007. In 1949 his remains were moved into the church, where they can still be visited.

The first Mount Argus was a tall red-brick house on a few acres through which the Poddle “lazed”. It belonged to Mrs Elizabeth Byrne, a widow and a cousin of Cardinal Cullen. At the suggestion of Father Matthew Collier, a curate in Rathmines, and with the Cardinal’s consent, the Passionists set up their house there in 1856. The old house and its temporary church stood where the community’s cemetery is now. The first Mass was said in August 1856 by Father Paul Mary Pakenham, a son of the second Earl of Longford, who had been a captain in the British Army before he became a Catholic. Source: Irish Independent, 16 October 1956. Show The first Mount Argus on the map →

Loader’s Park Mill stood beside the grounds of Mount Argus. A “C. Mill”, a corn mill, is marked here on Rocque’s map of 1760; by 1843 it was a paper mill, and the 1911 Ordnance Survey map shows a corn mill again. The Gothic stone scout hall at the back entrance to Mount Argus, on Mount Argus Road, seems to have been part of the mill and was standing by 1843. Patrick Pearse is said to have taught Irish there. The ruined mill and a few small cottages, perhaps for the mill workers, survived until the late 20th century. Show Loader’s Park Mill on the map →

Kimmage Road Lower runs from Kimmage Cross Roads to Harold’s Cross Road. The first Ordnance Survey map, of 1837, shows cottages along it, and the terraces at its northern end were built in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. The river runs close beneath them. On a Saturday in February 1910 the Poddle overflowed on high ground near Mount Argus and poured down the Upper and Lower Kimmage roads, three or four feet deep in places. The Rathmines township sent a “float” that spent the evening ferrying people “from shore to shore”. In March 1937 the fire brigade was pumping out houses here again. On 29 November 1985 Maureen Cooke opened her front door at 9 Kimmage Road to find a hole ten feet square where part of her garden had been. The culvert carrying the river, less than six feet under the front gardens, had collapsed. Source: Irish Independent, 21 February 1910; Irish Press, 13 March 1937 and 30 November 1985. Stop 11 of 18 · Harold’s Cross Mount Jerome A Victorian cemetery, perhaps another monks’ diversion, and a siphon under the canal. In brief A Victorian cemetery beside the river, where it goes underground and then dips under the Grand Canal in a siphon.

The General Cemetery Company of Dublin was set up by Robert Shaw under an Act of Parliament in 1834. The first burial took place on 19 September 1836, and there have been about 250,000 since. As one of Dublin’s main cemeteries it holds many graves of historical interest, among them those of John Millington Synge and Jack B. Yeats.

To enter Mount Jerome, the Poddle makes an almost right-angled turn. In his 1927 paper, Rev. Myles Ronan asks whether this was another diversion of the original river, again made for St Thomas’s Abbey, this time to serve its mills. For that reason this stretch is sometimes called the Abbey Stream, though it is more often just called the Poddle, as it carries most of the river’s water. The map page shows the Abbey Stream, which leaves the Poddle just downstream of here, as an amber band.

A flour mill once stood near the cemetery gates. Just downstream, the Poddle powered Greenmount Mills. A corn mill on the site was turned into a cotton mill by James Greenham by 1807, and in the mid-19th century the Quaker Pim family enlarged it, making cotton and linen; the Pims were also known for Irish poplin. The mill pond survived until it was covered over in the late 1960s. Our Lady’s Hospice, founded in 1845 by Mother Mary Aikenhead, stands on the river’s banks at Harold’s Cross, and the 1910 Ordnance Survey map shows another mill pond in its grounds. In the October 2011 floods, a nurse from the hospice lost her life.

The stream enters the cemetery behind the Russian Orthodox Church of the Holy Apostles Peter and Paul, flows under the cemetery’s entrance road and then along its eastern boundary. From here it is culverted under Greenmount, and it passes beneath the Grand Canal in a siphon. Dublin Corporation’s minutes for 1972 record a £35,000 loan for culverting the river between Greenmount Lane and the Grand Canal.

Just past Greenmount the river meets the Grand Canal, close to Robert Emmet Bridge, which most people call Harold’s Cross Bridge. The canal was dug straight across the Poddle’s path in the 1790s, and ever since then the river has had to find a way underneath it. Weston St John Joyce, writing in 1912, describes it going “under the canal at Goodbody’s factory”. It does it with a siphon: a pipe that dips down below the canal bed and comes up again on the far side. In 2003 archaeologists watching groundworks at 25 Parnell Road, beside the canal, looked down a manhole and found a fast-flowing watercourse at least five metres below the surface. They took it to be the culverted Poddle, running deep enough to pass beneath the canal. How the siphon works. A simplified drawing, not to scale.

Water always tries to find its own level. If a pipe dips down and comes back up again, and its far end is a little lower than its near end, the pipe fills right up and stays full. Every bit of water that flows in at the top pushes the same amount out at the other end, so the river keeps moving without any pump at all. Engineers call this an inverted siphon, because it dips down under an obstacle instead of going up and over it, like the tube used to empty a fish tank. It has two drawbacks. Silt and rubbish settle at the lowest point and have to be cleared, and fish can’t easily get through. The flood scheme’s ecologists name the siphon as one of the barriers that keep trout and eels out of the Poddle.

The structure there now is described as late 20th century. Around the time of the 1972 culverting, Dublin Corporation was also digging the Grand Canal Tunnel, a sewer 4.8 km long and 3.6 metres across that runs beside the canal towards Ringsend. One of its jobs, according to Dublin City Council, is to take storm water from the Poddle and the Swan River and so cut the risk of flooding. At the canal the Poddle has an overflow into this drainage pipe, so in a flood some of its water can escape there instead of backing up into Harold’s Cross. RTÉ reported in July 1975 that the tunnel had taken two and a half years to build and cost £4 million. The City Watercourse had a crossing of its own, just east of Dolphin’s Barn Bridge. A newspaper report of a flood in March 1937 says that the stream then ran underground for 400 yards from above Rutland Cottages and emptied into the canal near the bridge. Today the Grand Canal Tunnel intercepts it there. We still don’t know how the Grand Canal Company carried the river across when the canal was first dug in the 1790s, or who did the work. Harold’s Cross was a small village south of the city until the middle of the 18th century; Rocque’s map of 1760 shows houses clustered around its green. It grew quickly in the late 18th and early 19th centuries with the Grand Canal, and Taylor’s map of 1816 and Duncan’s of 1821 show terraces along Harold’s Cross Road. The wedge-shaped park in the middle is the old village green and medieval common, which stayed open ground until the Rathmines Township Commissioners laid out the present park in 1893 and 1894. Harold’s Cross had its mills too: a sketch of the old Harold’s Cross laundry shows its water wheel in the Poddle. Source: Kimmage BusConnects scheme documentation. Mount Jerome is named after the Rev. Stephen Jerome, a 17th-century preacher and vicar of St Kevin’s. The lands had belonged to St Thomas’s Abbey; after the abbey was dissolved they passed to the Brabazons, later Earls of Meath, and the house was later home to the Wilkinsons and the Keoghs. The General Cemetery Company bought the 47-acre estate in 1836 and modelled the cemetery on Highgate in London. It was mainly a Protestant burial ground at first. By the late 20th century it was badly neglected and went into voluntary liquidation in 1984; new owners took over in 1998 and opened a crematorium in 2000. Behind the Russian Orthodox church by the cemetery gates there is a short open stretch of the river with some interesting old stonework, before it follows the cemetery wall and goes into its culvert. The Poddle, the Abbey Stream and the Tenter Water all pass under the Grand Canal, and in the 20th century the canal and the river were caught up in the same plans. In 1961 Dublin Corporation’s Streets Committee proposed using the line of the canal for a new sewer to Ringsend, and in October 1963 the City Engineer proposed turning the canal itself into a culvert with a sewer beside it, together with the “long-overdue” culverting of the Poddle from Kimmage Manor. Canal societies objected, and in the end the Grand Canal Tunnel was laid beside the canal instead. In the early 1970s the Corporation asked for £35,000 to culvert the river. Eventually, it said, the whole 1,000 metres from south of Kimmage Manor to the canal would have to go underground; the urgent part was the 240 metres from Greenmount Lane to the canal, whose walls were weak and at risk of collapse in places. The canal has its own memories of the river. On the Night of the Big Wind, 6 January 1839, trees along the canal banks were torn up, a boat capsized in Portobello Harbour, and the Poddle burst over its banks. Stop 12 of 18 · Clanbrassil Street and Warrenmount Blackpitts Tanners’ pits, mill streams and a river that marked a boundary. In brief North of the canal the river runs underground past Warrenmount to Blackpitts, a district of tanners and mills named after the pits along the stream.

North of the Grand Canal, the culverted river runs along Clanbrassil Street, past Donore Avenue, Warrenmount and Blackpitts. Blackpitts, a name on maps by 1728, probably comes from the pits used by tanners along the river, and Mill Street, first mentioned in 1711, recalls a double mill for oil and flour that is linked to St Thomas’s Abbey. In 1830 the street had several tanners and a fancy weaver; by 1880 it had five tanners and a parchment maker. During a great fire on 22 June 1875, burning whiskey ran into the Poddle beneath Ardee Street and set the river alight. One account of the area, on the Hidden Dublin website, describes a man-made side channel at Blackpitts that came from the direction of Ardee Street, turned east along Sweeney’s Lane and then north to join the main river; it was photographed in 2007, on a site then about to be built over. Faddle Alley, a lane off Blackpitts, is where the blind street rhymer Michael Moran, known as Zozimus, was born in about 1794. He died in lodgings on Patrick Street, also on the river’s course, in 1846. Near New Row it picks up its ancient course again, and at the junction of New Street, Patrick Street and Kevin Street, the old Cross Poddle (renamed Dean Street by the Wide Streets Commissioners in 1826), a medieval mill stood on its bank beside St Nicholas’ Bridge, outside St Nicholas’ Gate. At Fumbally Lane it is joined by the Tenter Water, a branch of the City Watercourse, and at the corner of the Coombe and Patrick Street by its one real tributary, the Commons Water, which rises in Crumlin.

Cross Poddle was much older than its mill. In the Middle Ages it was the lowest point at which the Poddle could be forded, so several important roads met there, with a gate outside the city walls and a market. The area may already have been settled before the Normans came, with several early churches and possibly an Irish suburb of the Norse town. Just upstream, the river gave Blackpitts its trade. In 2004 archaeologists excavating at 48 New Street South found more than a hundred tanning pits, dating from the late 13th century to the 17th. The archaeologist Antoine Giacometti argues that this was not one big tannery but a quarter of small household tanyards, worked behind the houses on New Street. Tanners needed a steady supply of water to soak and rinse hides, and late medieval records show ditches being dug off the Poddle to serve the tanneries. From the 15th century, laws often ordered those ditches filled in, because the Poddle kept flooding and the tanners were fouling the water. The site ran along the top of a steep slope down into the Poddle valley. A ditch dug along it in the 13th or 14th century ran into or out of the river near a medieval millpond, which was excavated just north-west of the site. The millpond was dug in the 13th or 14th century and filled in during the 14th or 15th, the same dates as the ditch, which may have been its tail race or overflow. Giacometti suggests both were part of the great programme of works in the mid-13th century, when the river was diverted round the Liberties and mills and water channels were set along its old and new courses, marking the edges of the church lands. Disputes over those mills and watercourses fill the medieval records. Rows of tanning pits uncovered during an archaeological excavation at Blackpitts. Photo courtesy of Reddit user Few_shine2208. Donore Avenue was once Love Lane, and the Poddle ran open beside it. Dublin Corporation’s printed reports for 1901 (Report No. 129 of the Paving Committee, pages 301 to 316) tell the story of how it came to be covered. In 1894 an architect, Robert Stirling, laid out new roads on the Huband estate off the South Circular Road, reached through Love Lane. The Borough Surveyor, Spencer Harty, agreed to narrower roads on condition that a stretch of the Poddle he marked “A” was covered over: “this will be a great improvement.” The Corporation approved this in 1896, but the new road was never built, so the river was never covered. By 1900 the residents had had enough. A petition forwarded by the Rev. Fergus Greer, rector of St Catherine’s, and signed by the Greenmount Spinning Company and “a great many others” pointed out “the great danger and nuisance the Poddle River is to the public, when it is exposed to the open, adjoining the street, now known as Donore Avenue, formerly Love Lane.” The lane was “only 10 feet wide alongside the river”, wide enough for one vehicle at a time, and there was “the added danger to children from the narrow thoroughfare and the open river, especially now when it is contemplated building a parish school alongside the river.” Harty reported that covering about 320 feet of the river would give a road 25 feet wide with two 6-foot footpaths, for about £1,850. The Huband estate’s new agent refused to pay for its share, and the Law Agent advised that if the river was to be covered, the Corporation was the proper authority to do it. On 31 July 1901 the Paving Committee agreed the work “would be an improvement”, but “considering the pressing demand on the funds of the Corporation at this present time”, it would not recommend spending £1,850. The Corporation’s index shows a loan of £1,850 for covering the Poddle at Donore Avenue the following year, so the work went ahead in 1902. Today, according to McEntee and Corcoran, the old course is blocked off outside Donore Avenue church and a newer culvert carries the flow along Donore Avenue, rejoining the old route between Ebenezer Terrace and Harman Street before it reaches the old mill pond at Warrenmount.

St Kevin’s National School for boys, built in 1894 and 1895 and opened on 20 April 1895, faces onto Blackpitts. Its site follows the old course of the Poddle, which was also an old boundary: on one side the lands of St Thomas’s Abbey, later the Earl of Meath’s Liberty, and on the other those of St Patrick’s Cathedral, later the Liberty of St Sepulchre. The lanes off Blackpitts have their own stories. Dowker’s Lane was once Tucker’s Lane. Warrenmount is named after Nathaniel Warren, Lord Mayor in 1782 and an MP for the city, who was rumoured to be a partner in “The Sham”, a notorious gambling house. Fumbally Lane had Barnatt’s food stores in an old brewery building, where fire broke out on the morning of 15 September 1906; the brigade had it out within an hour.

Much of the housing around Blackpitts was built in the 1880s by Arthur Hammond, a Catholic builder. His daughter, Mary Agnes Hammond, inherited 150 houses in 1902; she is remembered as a British spy during and after the First World War. Many of her tenants worked at the Guinness brewery, and the deeds of her houses carried an unusual right: to wash in the River Poddle, long after it had gone underground. She never married and died in Switzerland in 1956. Her estate of 26 terraced houses in Blackpitts, Emerald Square and Dolphin’s Barn was still largely together when it was sold in the 1980s. Stop 13 of 18 · New Row and Dean Street Cross Poddle Where six streets met at the old crossing of the river. In brief The Poddle’s old crossing at Dean Street, once called Cross Poddle, and the covered channels known as the Poddle Hole.

New Row, once “New Row on the Poddle”, runs between Blackpitts and the Coombe. The river passes behind its buildings and those of New Street. Its newspaper history is lively. On 12 September 1730 two sharpers who had just robbed a man fell out over the purse in New Row; one was killed and the other badly beaten, and the victim never saw his money again. In November 1787 the Poddle flooded houses from New Row to Meath Street, driving people into their upper rooms. The storm of 12 June 1822 brought down chimneys in New Row and Malpas Street, and on the Night of the Big Wind in 1839 a falling chimney killed a mother and child in New Row. In the days of the Penal Laws, Catholic lay teachers such as Catherine Anderson and Catherine Hanley kept illegal schools in New Row. Show New Row on the Poddle on the map →

Dean Street, where Patrick Street, New Street and Kevin Street meet, was called Cross Poddle until May 1826, when the Wide Streets Commissioners renamed it. Rocque’s map of 1756 simply marks it “Poddle”, as do the Pool and Cash map of the 1780s and maps of 1787 and 1797; the first map found with “Cross Poddle” is an 1818 plan of the precincts of St Patrick’s Cathedral. The “Cross” may refer to church lands or to the crossing of the stream itself. It was a bottleneck less than 25 feet wide where six streets met. In 1814 a resident wrote to the Paving Board that snow had blocked it so badly that carriages could neither pass nor turn, and suggested that if every householder, the dairymen included, took away one cartful, the street would be clear in two hours. Where New Street, Patrick Street and Dean Street meet was once Freestone Alley, later Freeman’s Stone; a stone here is recorded in 1603 as marking the boundary between the city and the archbishop’s liberty. Punishment was public. In 1766 Dennis Sullivan was whipped from Cross Poddle to Harold’s Cross for stealing meal, with a bag of meal tied round his neck, on the order of Mr Justice Drury. Source: Faulkner’s Dublin Journal, 1766; Rocque (1756); 19th-century plan of St Patrick’s precincts. Show Cross Poddle on the map →

The Poddle Hole was the name for the covered channels of the river near St Patrick’s Cathedral, and things turned up in it. On a Sunday evening in September 1770, “to the amazement of many people”, several hundred live herrings were taken out of the Poddle Hole water under the house at the Sign of the Royal Oak at Nicholas’ Gate. In October 1789 drinkers in a tavern in Essex Street heard roaring under their kitchen and found a young bull trapped beneath the flags over the Poddle channel. It was rescued; nobody claimed it, and it was thought to have been swept in at the Poddle Hole. To give someone a “Poddle Hole step” was to plunge your foot into the gutter and splash them. When rioters from Cavan were carted through the Liberty to be punished in November 1735, one of them gave the hangman a Poddle Hole step, which earned him a harder beating. Source: Dublin Chronicle, 13 September 1770 and 1 October 1789; Dublin Evening Post, 15 November 1735. Show The Poddle Hole on the map →

Kevin Street Garda Station stands on the site of the archbishops’ palace of St Sepulchre, built in the late 12th century by John Comyn, the first Norman archbishop of Dublin. Its name recalls the Crusades and the Holy Sepulchre in Jerusalem. It stood near the Slighe Chualann, the old road south, and the archbishops’ lands stretched from Harold’s Cross to Donnybrook and Crumlin; by the 14th century there were mills on the Poddle and houses all around. The palace was damaged in the Bruce invasion of 1315. It is often said the river was part of its defences, though no map has been found to show it; the archbishop’s grounds did once reach as far as Cross Poddle. In 1806 it was handed to the government and became a police barracks, later the headquarters of the Dublin Metropolitan Police. A 16th-century window and parts of the vaulted kitchens survive. In 1751 William Jackson, a butcher from Kevin Street, was shot climbing the palace garden wall after a run of thefts. Days later his family and a crowd stormed the house to find the man who fired, and it took the Poddle Guard, called out by Justice Drury, to stop them. Show St Sepulchre’s Palace on the map →

Bishop Street dates from about 1610. It was Butter Lane, then Boater Lane by 1756, and took its present name in 1774, probably from the archbishop who owned it. Old maps show a watch house at its Kevin Street end, near St Patrick’s Well and the river. It is often said the Poddle ran under Jacob’s biscuit factory here, and a newspaper once told of two workers who fished in it on quiet shifts, but no map evidence has been found that the river ever flowed under the factory. Stop 14 of 18 · Patrick Street St Patrick’s Cathedral Built between two streams, and flooded by them for centuries. In brief The cathedral was built on an island between two streams, and the river flooded it for centuries.

Near Patrick Street the Poddle once ran in two channels, one on each side of the street, joining again near Bride’s Alley before turning east towards the Castle. The first church of St Patrick stood on the island of dry ground between them, which is why the Normans called it St Patrick’s “in insula”, on the island. It was a holy site and a very wet one. Tradition says that St Patrick baptised converts at a well here in the fifth century. The first record of a church on the site is from 890. The cathedral’s own account says that in 1901, during building works beside it, six carved grave slabs were found, and one of them was lying over what looked like an old well; other accounts date the find to the middle of the 19th century. The carving is dated to around the tenth century. The cathedral describes this as possibly, not certainly, the well of the story. The stone is now kept inside the cathedral, and a plaque in the park marks the reputed site of the well. The architect Sir Thomas Drew left a more exact note, quoted by Ronan in 1927. On 16 June 1901, he wrote, the site of the well was found “in course of opening up the old arched course of the Poddle on the east side of Patrick Street by Spencer Harty, City Surveyor, to build a new tunnel (with concrete)”. It was marked by “an ancient granite stone marked with two crosses in high, clear relief”, built into the side of the old culvert, and the stone was taken into the cathedral on 19 June 1901. Drew and Harty thought the well itself had been lost when the river was diverted, probably under Charles II, into a great stone culvert along the cathedral’s west front to drive a corn mill there, the mill that gave Cross Poddle its name.

John Comyn, the first Norman archbishop of Dublin, made the little church collegiate in 1191, with a body of clergy for worship and learning, and dedicated it on 17 March that year. His successor, Henry de Loundres, raised it to a cathedral; most accounts date this to about 1212 or 1213, and in 1220 he created the office of dean. The great stone church we see was built in the following decades, between about 1220 and 1270 by most counts, with the Lady Chapel added around 1270. Building on an island in a river had a lasting cost. In the 20th century the water table was found to be within about 2.3 metres (seven and a half feet) of the floor, which is why the cathedral has never had a crypt, unlike Christ Church a few hundred metres away on its ridge above the Liffey.

The cathedral flooded again and again. There was an inquiry into blockages near it as early as 1437, and Parliament ordered local people to keep the drains clear in 1493 and again in 1664. In 1701 the flooding was so bad that people could row a boat past the cathedral, and in 1744 services had to move to Christ Church. Major floods followed in 1778, 1791 and 1795, and one in the early 19th century left about five feet of water inside the building. Weston St John Joyce noted that the city streams often spilled over the low ground of the Liberties and into the cathedral precincts, doing considerable damage. Ronan, writing in 1927, says that “on several occasions the water rose in the Cathedral as high as five feet and boats plied in Patrick Street”, and lists Acts of Parliament against the nuisance in 1437, 1493, 1664, 1687, 1701, 1762, 1778, 1796 and 1840. In November 1787 a Dublin newspaper reported that “the inhabitants from the end of New Street to Bride’s Alley were necessitated to keep to the upper apartments.”

A Dublin Corporation map reproduced by Rev. Myles Ronan in 1927 shows how the water around the cathedral was gradually tamed. The two arms of the Poddle run along Patrick Street, with St Patrick’s Well marked beside the cathedral. Between the cathedral and Bride Street, the old open ditches between Bull Alley, Bride’s Alley and Ross Lane are marked “ditch piped” and “brick built”, with a brick culvert running across to the river. The canons’ houses and gardens, the Chantor’s Manse, the Treasurer’s House and the Chantor’s Orchard, sat in the middle of this network of drains.

By the 1860s the river had become an open sewer, blamed for disease as well as flooding, and its lower reaches were roofed over. Dublin Corporation’s minutes show the work going on in the Liberties at the start of the 20th century: the Donore Avenue covering above, then loans in 1902 and 1903 for covering, repairing and underpinning it. Under Charles II a Poddle Commission had been set up to manage it, with power to levy a Poddle tax; its powers passed in 1840 to the Paving Commissioners by one account, and to Dublin Corporation by Ronan’s. Ronan lists the brick culverts that followed: Bride’s Alley in 1868, Bull Alley in 1870, the Close in 1872 and St Patrick’s Place in 1880 to 1882. Accounts differ on Patrick Street itself. One source says the street got its brick culvert in the 1920s, but Sir Thomas Drew’s note shows the City Surveyor building “a new tunnel (with concrete)” on the east side of the street in June 1901. McEntee and Corcoran add that Patrick Street had a culvert on each side until about 1904, and that the abandoned western one was uncovered and photographed when the road was widened in the 1990s. The Guinness family changed the area twice. Benjamin Lee Guinness paid for the great restoration of the cathedral in 1860 to 1865, when it was feared the building might collapse. In 1901 his son Edward Cecil Guinness, Lord Iveagh, cleared the crowded houses to the north and laid out St Patrick’s Park, and it was during that work that the old slab and well were found. Newspapers of 1900 report that the Poddle’s own course was moved to make way for the new Bull Alley and Bride’s Alley buildings. In 1902 the Corporation passed a vote of thanks to Lord Iveagh for a gift of £1,400 towards the work of completing the river opposite St Patrick’s. The river shaped local life in smaller ways too. The rough ground by the cathedral was policed by the “Poddle Guard”, a party of about twenty soldiers stationed nearby from 1725, and an 18th-century insult for an unruly Liberties crowd was a splash in the Poddle Hole. These details, with the newspaper sources, are gathered by the Crumlin and Walkinstown History Group’s Poddle project.

Stand in St Patrick’s Park and you are standing roughly on the island between the two old streams. The Poddle still runs beneath Patrick Street, along the west side of the park, in its culvert on the way to the Castle. Inside the cathedral, look for the old well slab, and notice that there are no steps down: the floor is as low as the water will allow.

Shortly after noon on 14 September 1882, without a moment’s warning, one of the great buttresses of the north chancel fell, killing three people. The Freeman’s Journal blamed the river: the cathedral was built on the lowest ground in the city, and the Poddle beneath it kept water lodged around its foundations. When Dublin Corporation widened Patrick Street and laid a new sewer in 1990, the archaeologist Claire Walsh excavated the old bed of the Poddle between March and July. In April her team found 13th-century timber revetments, stout oak walls sunk along the river’s banks to hold back floods, carry water into the city and win dry land from the marsh around the cathedral. In July they found a 13th-century corn mill of wood and stone, about ten metres long, the first medieval mill found in the city; it worked until the 15th century, when the river was diverted. The dig also turned up leather shoes, 12th-century coins, bronze pins and burials, one in an old lime kiln. At Nicholas Street there was evidence of the town wall and its ditch, with a lime kiln older than the channelling of the Poddle in the late 12th century; along Patrick Street, early wattle fences against flooding, a cobbled road and a tanning pit. The site was recorded but not kept. Pat Wallace of the National Museum said it could add a great deal to our picture of medieval Dublin; the Corporation’s spokesman, Noel Carroll, said the dig was there to record the old river before the sewer went in. Source: newspaper reports, 26 April, 15, 16 and 17 July 1990. Show The 1990 dig: a medieval mill on the map →

Bull Alley Street runs from Bride Street to Patrick Street, with St Patrick’s Park along its south side. Around 1900 the Bride’s Alley district, the “Poddle Valley”, was some of the worst housing in Dublin, and some houses in Anderson’s Court and Patrick Street had collapsed into the river beneath them. Lord Iveagh paid for much of the rebuilding. The Corporation moved part of the Poddle so the new buildings would stand on firm ground, and rebuilt the old sewers that ran into it. The plan was for 29 blocks housing 210 families, in 112 three-room and 98 two-room flats. The two streams of the Poddle met again at the corner of Patrick Street and Dean Street, and from there the united river ran under Patrick Street, Ross Lane, Bride Street and Ship Street to the Castle. Stop 15 of 18 · Dublin Castle Ship Street Little A sheep market, and a ravine as deep as any dig in Dublin. In brief A street named for sheep, beside a ravine that is among the deepest digs in Dublin’s history.

Ship Street Little and Ship Street Great, which run along the southern walls of Dublin Castle, are named not after ships but after the sheep market once held here. The Irish name, Sráid na gCaorach, means Street of the Sheep. The Poddle arrives from the west and flows under Ship Street Little and the Ship Street gate of Dublin Castle.
Round the hill, not over it

Walk from St Patrick’s Cathedral to Dublin Castle and the ground rises steeply under your feet, up Patrick Street and Nicholas Street towards Christ Church. So how does a river make the same journey? The answer is that it doesn’t climb at all. It goes round. The old walled city stands on a ridge of glacial clay and gravel between the Liffey and the Poddle. Boreholes on a site between Ship Street Great and Chancery Lane found glacial till down to about 9 metres, with limestone bedrock beneath. St Patrick’s Cathedral was built below the ridge, on low, wet ground between branches of the river, which is why it has flooded so often. Christ Church was built on top of it. From the cathedral the Poddle ran north, parallel with Patrick Street, in two or more courses down the west and east sides of the street, as far as Ross Road and the line of the southern city wall. There, at the foot of the ridge, it turned east and ran along the walls and the castle ramparts, past Ship Street, around the Royal Chapel, and out at the Lower Castle Gate at Palace Street and Dame Street on its way to the Liffey. That is the route given in Clair Sweeney’s book The Rivers of Dublin, quoted in the 2018 engineering report for the Ship Street site. Water always takes the lowest line, and the lowest line from the Liberties to the Liffey runs round the eastern tip of the ridge, not over the top. It is better to think of it the other way round. The Poddle’s valley is what makes the southern and eastern edge of the ridge, and the 2020 dig below shows how deep that valley once was. The Normans built Dublin Castle on the end of the ridge, where the river and the Dubh Linn gave them a ready-made moat. You can still feel the valley today: Ship Street Little sits well below Werburgh Street and Castle Street, and the Forty Steps climb from Ship Street up to the level of the old city. How the Poddle goes round the ridge. A simplified drawing, not to scale; the river is culverted all the way today.

Archaeological excavations in 2020, on a site just south of Ship Street Little and west of Ship Street Great, found that the Poddle here once ran through a ravine that fed into the Dubh Linn. The ravine was so deep that, at the time of writing, it was the deepest archaeological excavation in the city’s history. Once the monks of St Thomas’s Abbey had diverted water away, the channel dried up, and the ravine was quarried for stone for the walls of the Norman castle.

Sister Ann Dominica Fitzgerald opened her 1973 essay “Down the Old Poddle” with a story from Ship Street. Condemned houses were being knocked down when the bulldozer “suddenly plunged through the surface into a void”, and the men peered down: “Be the hokey! An underground river!” The Corporation engineer who came down the steps at the back of Hoey’s Court had no doubt: “What you have there boys, is the Poddle. What else could it be in Ship Street?” The machine had broken through the arch of the Poddle, buried in the 1800s. Robert Mallet, the engineer who surveyed the river in 1844, described this last stretch the same way: from Warrenmount the water ran “in covered channels, known in the district by the name of the ‘Poddle Hole’ and passing near St. Patrick’s Cathedral, through Little Ship-street, the Castle-yard, and across Dame-street”, to the Liffey under Wellington Quay.

Boreholes sunk for the nearby Ship Street application in 2005 found made ground, soil built up by people, to between 3 and 5 metres down, glacial till to about 9 metres, and limestone bedrock between 7 and 9 metres down. The application includes a Dublin City Council drainage record map from March 2016, showing the sewers around Ship Street, Chancery Lane and Golden Lane. The sheet carries a warning that its accuracy must be checked on site.

Ship Street was split into Little and Great around 1700: Sir Bernard de Gomme’s map of 1673 shows a single street, and “Little Ship Street” appears in the will of Isaac Vauteau in 1711. Medieval records call it Vicus Ovinus. De Gomme’s map also shows a pool where Little and Great Ship Streets meet, and some have taken this pool, rather than the river, as the origin of the name Poddle. In 1678 the parish of St Andrew stated that the sea had once reached Ship Street, meeting the stream from the Pole Gate bridge, before the old harbour at Parliament Street was filled in. The hollow where the two streets meet is still there. One old writer remembered the river before it hid: in the days of Queen Elizabeth it “boldly entered the city at New Street, swept around St Patrick’s, washed the sides of the Castle, near Ship Street, and fell unconcernedly into the Liffey close to Dame’s Gate.” In January 1784 it did just that, rising six feet at the cathedral and covering Ship Street, the Lower Castle Yard and Dame Street as far as Sycamore Alley, before pouring through Crampton Court and Crane Lane into the Liffey. On the high ground above the river, where Great Ship Street now dips below Chancery Lane, stood the church of St Michael le Pole, with a round tower beside it. It took its name from the pool on the Poddle, which also gave its name to the Pole Gate in the city wall at St Werburgh Street. Tradition says it was founded by St Mac Táil in the 8th century, and a lintel grave found under it suggests worship here very early. Churches to St Michael were often built on high places. The church was deconsecrated in 1682 and was a school by 1706, the year a storm brought down the round tower; the rest was demolished in 1789 despite protests. Gabriel Beranger’s drawings record what it looked like. St Michael’s was one of a ring of early churches along the Poddle, with St Brigid’s in Bride Street, St Kevin’s, St Patrick’s “on the island” and St Nicholas’. Show St Michael le Pole on the map →

Under Archbishop Alexander de Bicknor (1317 to 1349) the parish of St Nicholas was split into St Nicholas Within the walls and St Nicholas Without. The outer parish took in both sides of Patrick Street, New Street and most of Kevin Street, and for a long time used the north transept of St Patrick’s as its church, walled off from the rest of the cathedral. In 1666 ground off Kevin Street was set aside as its burial ground, the Cabbage Garden. The transept was a ruin from 1784 until it was reroofed in 1825, and in 1861 the parish joined St Luke’s on the Coombe. In 1829 the householders of these parishes, St Nicholas Within and Without among them, met at the Tailors’ Hall about the Poddle Tax, which was charged on houses built over the river to keep its walls and arches in repair. Stop 16 of 18 · Dublin Castle gardens Dubh Linn The black pool that gave the city its name. In brief The black pool on the Poddle that gave Dublin its name now lies under the castle gardens.

The Dubh Linn, the black pool, was a pool on the Poddle just before it met the Liffey. The tidal, salty Liffey was no good for drinking, so the fresh water of the Poddle was the main drinking supply for the settlement that became Dublin. The pool may have been darkened by peat carried down from the hills. The Vikings who settled beside it called their town Dyfflin, from the Irish dubh linn. The pool itself lay under what are now the coach house and gardens of Dublin Castle.

As the city grew, the Poddle became a key defence on its southern side. The stream was channelled, and even dammed, to act as a moat. That dam is said to have given Dame Street, which now runs in front of Dublin Castle, its name. The moat had its weak points. Red Hugh O’Donnell’s escape from the Castle in the winter of 1591 to 1592 is traditionally said to have gone by way of the moat. He did not go alone: two fellow prisoners, Henry and Art O’Neill, sons of Shane O’Neill, got out with him, and the three headed south into the Wicklow mountains in deep snow. Art died of exposure there, and Red Hugh lost both his big toes to frostbite. In 1881 the Freeman’s Journal reported the authorities blocking the Poddle outfall, described as the only underground way into the Castle. In 1961 a tunnel about seven feet high was found under the Upper Yard.

Behind Dublin Castle, the site of the Dubh Linn is kept as a garden, a monument to its importance and the Poddle’s. The Dubh Linn Garden is bordered by the Chester Beatty Library, Dublin Castle and the Poddle, which now runs underground along its southern edge.

The heritage chapter of the flood scheme’s environmental report says the name Dublin, from Dubhlinn, black pool, is generally taken to refer to the pool that lay directly south-east of the present Dublin Castle, on the south side of the Liffey. It also notes a suggestion by the historian Clarke, in 1990, that Dubhlinn named an early Christian monastic settlement south of the pool. That would explain why the town has two names: Dubhlinn for the enclosed church settlement, and Baile Átha Cliath, the ‘ford of the hurdles’, for a secular settlement guarding the crossing.

The river that once filled the Castle moat now runs in a brick sewer under the roads around it. When the Castle was made ready for a state reception in June 1932, visitors walked in by the Cork Hill gate over the line of the old ditch, with the Poddle still running underneath. On the garden side, a small footbridge from the State Apartments crosses the line of the moat into the grounds that were the viceroy’s garden after 1700. Working in the river was dangerous. On 12 June 1913 John Roche, a labourer on the drainage works, had his right hand crushed while working in the Poddle in the Lower Castle Yard; blood poisoning followed. The Recorder awarded him £40 in compensation. On 2 February 1961 workmen probing for rock under Cork Hill broke into a tunnel seven feet high, only two feet below the road, bricked up at both ends and with a gas main laid over it. People wondered whether it was part of the old moat. Inside were five tons of coal, thought to explain a coal delivery that had gone missing years before down a forgotten manhole. Stop 17 of 18 · Dame Street Palace Street Under the castle gate, Dame Street and the Olympia. In brief The river leaves Dublin Castle by the Palace Street gate and runs north under Dame Street and the Olympia.

Inside the gates of Dublin Castle the river divides again. McEntee and Corcoran describe it: “Turning northwards opposite the Chapel Royal, the Poddle bifurcates inside the Palace Street Gate, the more westerly branch flowing under the open space beside City Hall before going under Dame Street. The eastern branch flows under Palace Street, beside a bank, which a gang of would-be robbers tried to access from the culvert in the 1980s.” The film Dublin’s Hidden Rivers shows that wall, from about 4:06 in (linked below), and the Media page has more on the 1985 raid. Rev. Myles Ronan, writing in 1927, gives an older version of the same split: past the Lower Castle Yard the Poddle “anciently divided again into two branches, one going by Exchange Court, Crane Lane, south side of Essex Street, to the bottom of Sycamore Street, where it met the other branch”. Sister Ann Dominica Fitzgerald’s 1973 plan of the river from Warrenmount to the Liffey shows the two channels crossing Dame Street and joining again by Essex Street East.

The river continues north under the Palace Street pedestrian gate of Dublin Castle and on to Dame Street. Dame Street takes its name from the dam on the Poddle, used both for defence and to power a mill.

From the castle gates the stream continues north, under Dame Street and beneath the historic Olympia Theatre. “Flowing under Dame Street and the Olympia Theatre,” McEntee and Corcoran write, “the main Poddle culvert is rejoined in Essex Street by its western or City Hall branch.”

People who have been down in the culverts here describe them differently, and none of this has been checked. One account, from an anonymous visitor shared on the Hidden Dublin website, says a side branch under the Olympia rejoins the main stream after about 100 metres, and that near the Record Tower a separate sewer runs alongside the river, taking its overflow when the water is high. The same account describes a stretch with a cobbled floor, thought to be among the oldest parts of the culvert, and says no sewage goes into the Poddle here and the water runs clear. Treat it as one person’s description, not a survey.

The Castle Yard flooded too. In November 1787 a Dublin newspaper reported that the people of Crampton Court and Palace Street “were put to distressing circumstances by the Poddle stream which breaking through its bounds in Lower Castle Yard inundated the houses of both places”. In 1814, McEntee and Corcoran record, the river was in spate when a boy working on an arch being built in the Castle Yard fell in. He was carried under Dame Street and Wellington Quay into the Liffey, and survived because the tide was out.
Into the Castle by the river

The culvert has always worried the Castle’s guardians. On 8 March 1921, during the War of Independence, Crown forces took George Harty, Dublin Corporation’s engineer in charge of sewers, to his office in an armoured car, made him hand over the drawings of the Poddle and the sewers near the Castle, and had him lead a British officer through a length of the culvert. Manholes along the route are still checked, and welded shut, before high-profile visits to the Castle.
Out of the Lower Castle Gate

The engineering report for the Ship Street development cites Clair Sweeney’s Rivers of Dublin, which says the exact historic line of the river through the city is not known, although the section through Dublin Castle is well documented. According to that account the river ran along the city walls and the castle ramparts, around the Royal Chapel, and out at the Lower Castle Gate at Palace Street and Dame Street.

The Olympia opened in 1879 as the Star of Erin Music Hall, the venture of Dan Lowrey. It became Dan Lowrey’s Music Hall in 1881, Dan Lowrey’s Palace of Varieties in 1889, the Empire Palace in 1897 and the Olympia in 1923. The river shaped the building: Lowrey wanted a Dame Street entrance and the stage in a different place, but the Poddle was in the way, so the audience reached the auditorium through a tunnel under the stage. In 1971 Dublin Corporation refused a plan to redevelop the site, partly because two branches of the river in culverts beneath it were higher than the proposed basements. A manhole in the theatre gives on to the river. In 1975 a newspaper recalled the story that Michael Collins’s men thought of it as an escape route during the War of Independence, though there is no evidence that anyone used it. Stop 18 of 18 · Wellington Quay Liffey Outfall Journey’s end, under Wellington Quay. In brief The Poddle ends its journey through an arch in the granite wall of Wellington Quay, built by the Wide Streets Commissioners between 1812 and 1815.

The Poddle’s journey ends here, flowing out under Wellington Quay into the Liffey through a grating in the quay wall, “an iron grid or portcullis”, as McEntee and Corcoran put it, “outside the Clarence Hotel”. The Liffey is tidal here, so at high tide the grating disappears under the water. Interestingly the Geological Survey Ireland, in its report on the Poddle as a County Geological Site, describes the grating as worn and dirty and suggests replacing it with stainless steel, spelling out “Poddle” in steel letters on the quay wall, and putting an information board on the far bank so people can see where Dublin’s first river meets the Liffey. Maybe that’s something worth considering for the future!

Wellington Quay was the last of the Liffey quays to be built. Until the early 1800s the houses along this stretch backed straight onto the river, and Faden’s map of 1797 still shows the riverside closed off by buildings. The Wide Streets Commissioners changed that. Between 1812 and 1815 they built a granite quay wall from Essex Bridge, now Grattan Bridge, to where the Ha’penny Bridge stands, to give the city a continuous quayside. Sources differ a little on the dates: one says the quay was built around 1812, another that it was laid out about 1815. The western end was already called Custom House Quay, after Thomas Burgh’s Custom House of 1704 to 1707. Gandon’s new Custom House took over its work in 1791, the old building was used partly as a barracks from 1798, and it was pulled down as the new quay went in. The Clarence Hotel now stands on much of its site. The quay is named after the Dublin-born Arthur Wellesley, 1st Duke of Wellington, after his victory over Napoleon at Waterloo in 1815, and it had its new name by 1817. The National Inventory of Architectural Heritage describes the Poddle’s outfall as an elliptical-headed culvert in the face of the wall. The arch probably dates from the building of the wall, when the river had to be carried out to the new quay line, but we haven’t found a source that says so.

On the new quay the Commissioners offered the Merchants’ Guild a site for a hall, on condition that a public right of way ran through it from Temple Bar to the Ha’penny Bridge. Frederick Darley designed the Merchants’ Hall, built in 1821 and 1822, and that passage is the Merchants’ Arch. It is one of only three guild halls left in the city.

At the east end of the quay is the Ha’penny Bridge. Before it was built, William Walsh ran seven ferries across the Liffey here. They were in such poor repair that he was told to fix them or build a bridge, and he chose the bridge. It opened in May 1816 as the Wellington Bridge, cast in 18 sections at Coalbrookdale in Shropshire. In return Walsh could charge a halfpenny toll for 100 years, collected at turnstiles at each end. The toll was dropped in 1919, and the bridge’s official name has been the Liffey Bridge since 1922.

Under the water off the quay lies Standfast Dick, sometimes called Steadfast Dick, a reef of rock in the bed of the Liffey that ran roughly from below Dublin Castle to Capel Street. Smaller ships coming up to the old Custom House kept getting stuck on it. In 1776 London ordered the channel deepened, and the Ballast Office set labourers “to quarry the bed of stones called Standfast near the Custom House”. They didn’t get all of it. In 1971 a newspaper reported that from the Wellington Quay wall at low tide you could still see the rock “extending far out into the bed of Anna Liffey”. James Joyce knew it too. In a 1927 draft of the Anna Livia Plurabelle chapter of Finnegans Wake he wrote of “a rise every morning for Standfast Dick and a drop every minute for Stumblestone Davy”.

In James Joyce’s Ulysses the outfall is placed, wrongly, at Wood Quay, in words that are unflattering but memorable: “From its sluice in Wood quay wall under Tom Devan’s office Poddle river hung out in fealty a tongue of liquid sewage.”

Dubliners have long claimed that “the River Saile” in the street song “Weila Waile”, made famous by The Dubliners on A Drop of the Hard Stuff (1967), is the Poddle, from its old Irish name the Salach, “the dirty river”. The song itself is traditional, an Irish form of the old ballad “The Cruel Mother”, and it is sung far beyond Dublin, sometimes with other river names. So the link is a cherished local tradition rather than a proven fact. Sources: Frank Hopkins, Hidden Dublin (Mercier Press, 2008), p. 147; Clare County Library song archive ( clarelibrary.ie ).
The gate at the river’s end

The quay was Custom House Quay until 1817. In 1881 workmen spent two days cutting through the outfall arch, then the only underground way into Dublin Castle, and fitted a high iron grille with heavy locks. Before that, it was said, the adventurous could walk the river’s bed between tides, past rats and foul smells, from the quay under Crampton Court, Dame Street, Exchange Court and Ship Street. The lower Poddle still runs in a large brick tunnel, and it has been said you can walk along it for almost three miles from Harold’s Cross; please don’t try. In the 1990s Temple Bar Properties proposed a copper-topped “Poddle bridge” for pedestrians here. 24 of the 42 councillors voted for it, but it needed a three-quarters majority because it conflicted with the city’s development plan, and it fell. History · c. 840 onwards At the heart of Dublin Drinking water, defence and power for the medieval city. In brief The Poddle gave medieval Dublin its drinking water, part of its defences and the power for its mills.

The modest Poddle is the most historic river in Dublin. The clue is in the name: Dubh Linn, the black pool, was a pool on the stream just outside where Dublin Castle now stands. It was the city’s main source of drinking water, because the Liffey is tidal and brackish. It formed part of the city’s defences: Dame Street, one of the city’s main streets, is said to be named after the dam that turned the stream into a moat. And it powered the mills of the city’s industries and religious houses.

Dublin City Council’s presentation on the flood scheme says the Poddle once powered 52 mills and commercial enterprises along its course, and that it has 15 associated watercourses. Today most of its last stretch runs underground. The Ship Street planning report puts the culverted or piped length at about 4 km through the city, and says the river’s exact historic line is not known.

History · Source to sea Origins Why a small stream ended up at the centre of the city. In brief A small stream from the Dublin Mountains ended up running through the middle of the city.

The stream rises in the foothills of the Dublin Mountains. Its catchment is bounded by the Dodder to the south and the Camac to the north. Both of those rivers are larger than the Poddle, but the Poddle is the one that runs to the heart of the city, while its neighbours pass to the east and west of the centre. Its route is what puts the Poddle at the heart of Dublin, physically and in its history. Today almost all of its last four kilometres, under the south inner city, runs in culverts. Geologically it is a young river. Geological Survey Ireland lists the Poddle as a County Geological Site for Dublin City, noting that it formed after the last Ice Age, within roughly the last 11,000 years, on low-permeability glacial till. The survey picks it out because so much of its course runs in man-made channels and tunnels underground, which is unusual in Ireland.

The river rises around Cookstown, north-west of Tallaght, about 92 metres above sea level, where its first stretch is known as the Tymon River. Its catchment covers about 16 square kilometres, almost all of it now built up. The name has changed over the centuries: Podell in 1493, Puddell in 1603, and Poddle from 1695. In Irish it is An Poitéal, and it was also called the Salach, the dirty river. Other names turn up in local histories, among them Glascholach and Cam Uisce, the crooked stream, which has been suggested, without certainty, as the origin of the name Kimmage.

The river has also been written Pottle, and even, grandly, the Tiber, and in Irish Soulagh or Salach, the dirty one. It left its mark on the language of the Liberties: The Poddle Act : “An Act for preventing the Inundations of the Poddle River in Dublin, and for preserving the Cathedral Church of Saint Patrick and the Houses of the adjoining Inhabitants from the Damages arising therefrom” (1840). Read it on the Irish Statute Book . The Poddle Tax : paid by houses built over the river, to keep its walls and arches in repair; later charged too on houses that drained into it. A Poddle Hole step : a sudden plunge of the foot in the gutter, to splash whoever was nearest. The Poddle Guard : a party of about twenty soldiers kept at a barracks near St Patrick’s from 1725. History · Before 1244 The first diversion Turning the Dodder into the Poddle at Balrothery. In brief Before 1244 the monks of St Thomas’s Abbey dug a channel to bring water from the Dodder into the Poddle.

The first great change was the diversion of water from the Dodder into the Poddle at Balrothery Weir, near Firhouse. It was a remarkable piece of engineering. Some 10km from St Thomas’s Abbey, a weir was built across the Dodder and a new channel dug that carried most of the river’s ordinary flow for about 3km to join the Poddle near Mount Down, in Kimmage. It was done for two reasons. More water meant more power for the Abbey’s mills, and it gave the Abbey and the city a larger and steadier supply of drinking water, which was stored in a cistern outside James’s Gate, on what is now Thomas Street. The system ran for around 500 years.

The first firm date is 29 April 1244, when the justiciar, Maurice Fitzgerald, ordered the sheriff of Dublin to find out, “by twelve free and lawful men”, where water could best be taken “and conducted to the King’s city of Dublin, for the benefit of the city and at the cost of the citizens”. Anyone who got in the way could be arrested. The Dodder weir was chosen, enlarged and repaired, and in 1245 the King ordered water piped to his new hall in Dublin Castle by the following summer. Who built the weir in the first place is less certain. Most accounts say the monks of St Thomas’s had it before 1244 and the citizens enlarged it. Others date the watercourse to between 1245 and 1254, or the weir itself to 1254, and one reading of the evidence puts the weir as early as the late 12th century. The Balrothery Weir page sets these out side by side.

The city and the Abbey had to share. Under their agreement the city paid for works on the monks’ weir on the Dodder, and the Abbey was paid a mark and a yearly rent of five marks, though the payments were sometimes late or missed. A public cistern outside James’s Gate is recorded supplying citizens in 1254, and a second conduit was built at the Cornmarket by the mayor John Le Decer in 1308. Further down, at Harold’s Cross, the combined stream was split again by the Tongue, so that one third went to the city and two thirds to the Abbey mills. That is the second diversion .

Ironically, the CFRAM Poddle options report of the 2000s examined an option for flood relief: “A suitable diversion route has been identified from the Poddle to the Dodder along Tymon Park running south of the M50.” Eight centuries after the monks turned the Dodder into the Poddle, the engineers proposed sending it back.

The heritage chapter of the flood scheme’s environmental report dates the channel from Balrothery, near Firhouse, to about 1244, with the Firhouse weir possibly as early as the late 12th century. A 1244 inquisition ordered by the justiciar Maurice Fitzgerald looked at how to bring more water to Dublin, and the Dodder weir was enlarged. History · 1245 The second diversion The Stone Boat splits the river for St Thomas’s Abbey. In brief In 1245 the Stone Boat at Kimmage began splitting the river to send water to St Thomas’s Abbey.

The second diversion was no less ingenious. In 1245, at what is now Harold’s Cross, the stream was split by the Tongue, a stone shaped like the bow of a boat and known locally as the Stone Boat. It sent part of the Poddle’s water west to St Thomas’s Abbey. You can still see both diversions. The first is no longer used, but its workings can be seen at Balrothery, near Tymon Park, just outside the M50. The Tongue, or Stone Boat, is still in the river near Mount Argus.

In 1245 the King directed John FitzGeffrey to finish his hall in the castle and to bring water to it by the summer of 1246. A 1259 inquisition records an agreement between the monks of St Thomas’s and the citizens to make the new watercourse. The heritage chapter, drawing on H. F. Berry in 1891, says the watercourse was built in the middle of the 13th century, with its head at Balrothery. It flowed north-east, skirting the churchyard wall at Templeogue, and was joined by the Poddle at Mount Down Flour Mills. From there the two ran as one stream to the Tongue at Kimmage. s: History · 1245 to 1324 The City Watercourse and the Abbey Stream Two channels made for the monks and the city, and how to find them on the map. In brief Two man-made channels carried the river’s water to the abbey and the city; here is how to find them on the map.

The City Watercourse is an artificial channel. At the Stone Boat, in Harold’s Cross, it took one third of the river’s water: two thirds stayed in the Poddle and one third went into the watercourse, which carried it north-west towards Dolphin’s Barn. Near today’s Basin Lane it turned east along the south side of James’s Street and through Thomas Street into the city. It was the city’s main water supply for centuries, which is why the 1719 Act of Parliament was written to keep it clean and to stop mill owners starving it of water. A branch of it, the Tenter Water, rejoined the Poddle at Fumbally Lane. The Poddle’s one real tributary, the Commons Water, came in from Crumlin along the Cork Street area and joined it near the Coombe; both are drawn, approximately, on the map. On the map page the City Watercourse is shown as a dashed red line, from Balrothery Weir to the Stone Boat and on to Christ Church. As far as Dolphin’s Barn it follows lines drawn from old Ordnance Survey maps: the channel crossed the Grand Canal just east of Dolphin’s Barn Bridge and ran north up the Back of the Pipes, behind Reuben Street, as the 1909 Ordnance Survey sheets show. The stretches above Mount Down and north of the Back of the Pipes are drawn from a local hand-drawn map with no stated source. Treat all of it as approximate.

The scheme began with an inquiry. In April 1244 the justiciar, Maurice FitzGerald, ordered a search for a new water supply for Dublin, and the city came to an arrangement with St Thomas’s Abbey to take water from the Dodder at Balrothery. The work went on, by most accounts, from 1245 to 1324. From the basin near James’s Street the water ran along Thomas Street and High Street to a conduit at Christ Church and the Tholsel. Householders could tap it, but private lead pipes were supposed to be no thicker than a goose quill. In 1308 the mayor, John le Decer, paid for a marble cistern at Cornmarket, and iron mains began to replace the old pipes from 1802. In November 1970 the Evening Herald reported timber water pipes, perhaps 250 years old, dug up at Weaver’s Square.

In the early 1970s the City Watercourse between Firhouse and Kimmage was threatened by new building. A Dominican nun, Sister Ann Dominica Fitzgerald, walked its length, fell into the Poddle twice while tracing it, and called herself a “Poddleologist”. She wrote to the papers in 1972 and 1973 to save the 700-year-old channel, and in 1976 led a Poddle tour for the Dublin Arts Festival, from Mount Argus to Warrenmount. Born in Blackrock, she taught at the Dominican convent at Muckross Park in Donnybrook and took her classes out on the river whenever she could. She photographed stretches of the watercourse before they disappeared, wrote the narration for a 16mm film of it made by John Gleeson of Inchicore, who also wrote to the papers to defend it, and contributed “Down the Old Poddle” to The Liberties of Dublin, edited by Elgy Gillespie (E. and T. O’Brien, 1973). Her interest began while she was writing a schools book on the Liffey and found there were no books on the subject. In a letter to the Irish Press on 1 May 1972 she wrote that she had gone back to re-photograph Mount Down Mill and found it razed. She died on 10 March 2006.

The Abbey Stream is the name given on modern maps to a channel that leaves the Poddle near the Hospice and Greenmount, at Harold’s Cross, and runs north-west towards St Thomas’s Abbey. Rev. Myles Ronan’s 1927 map marks a “course of ancient water” heading the same way, across the fields east of the river. Between 1245 and 1324 the monks redirected the river’s course to serve their mills, and this is the kind of channel that diversion would have made. At Mount Jerome the Poddle itself makes an almost right-angled turn, and Ronan asked whether that too was a diversion made for the abbey. On the map page the Abbey Stream is the amber band; its middle section is under streets, so the link across it is a straight, approximate line.

Older writers describe the two branches at the Tongue in detail. The branch that became the Poddle’s city course ran by Greenmount, under the canal, then by Blackpitts, New Row and Patrick Street to the castle and the Liffey. The City Watercourse proper ran to Dolphin’s Barn and along an embankment called the Pipes to the city basin near James’s Street. A cistern was built near the old reservoir around 1670. The planning file page has the full record.

The two are easy to confuse. The City Watercourse leaves the river at the Stone Boat, upstream. The Abbey Stream leaves it further down, at Harold’s Cross, and both were made to serve the abbey and the city.

When Henry VIII closed St Thomas’s Abbey in 1538 its lands, with “a malt mill, a wood mill and two double mills”, went to Sir William Brabazon, ancestor of the Earls of Meath. From then on the abbey’s channel through the Liberties was called the Earl of Meath’s Watercourse, and the Earls controlled water supply and charges in their Liberty for more than three centuries. Dublin Corporation eventually bought those rights, though even one book gives two versions: McEntee and Corcoran say in one chapter that it was in 1864 for £6,400, and in another that it was in 1861 for £6,000. The Earl kept the land, the river bed and banks, and the right to use the water for mills. A reservoir built for him around 1820, the Liberty Basin at Pim Street, was built over in Victorian times and uncovered again in 2006. See the Mount Jerome turn on the river walk →

History · 1719 The 1719 Act Parliament acts to clean up the city’s water. In brief In 1719 Parliament ordered the watercourse cleaned, because mills, dyers and tanners were fouling and draining it.

An Act of Parliament of 1719 describes the watercourse as “the chief supply of water not only for the inhabitants of the said city; but also for this majesties Castle of Dublin, and without which it would suffer exceeding great prejudice.” The Act provided for cleaning and repairing the watercourse, because: “…tuck mills, in which urine, soap and other unwolsome materials are made use of, and diers of linnen and woolen cloath and yarn, and skinners dip, wash, scour and cleanse great quantities of died linnen and woolen cloath, yarn and skins in the said water-course, by which the water is greatly corrupted, endangering the healths of the inhabitants of the said city.” Original 1719 spelling Mills along the watercourse were also a problem, building dams and ponds that blocked the flow of water into the city.

McEntee and Corcoran explain the background. In 1718 there were complaints about effluent from a tuck mill and a paper mill on the watercourse, and the mill owners argued that the Corporation had no power to stop them. The Act, “for cleaning and repairing the watercourse from the River Dodder to the City of Dublin, and to prevent the diverting and corrupting the Water therein”, gave the Corporation full control. It also outlawed tuck mills and woollen mills on the Poddle and the City Watercourse. Mount Down Mill, near Kimmage, was one that had to change: it had been a woollen mill, and after the Act it was turned over to grinding flour. The rules were not new. A Corporation order of 1538 had already said that “no manner person may wash foul clothes … and no man cast no corrupt thing in the same water, as blood of swyne or kyne … nor wash tripes or puddings there”, on pain of a fine of twelve pence.

The Poddle and the City Watercourse remained the city’s only public water supply until 1745, when a pump on the Liffey at Islandbridge began to serve the north side. Water from the Grand Canal began to replace the Poddle at the City Basin in 1775 by most accounts (Fitzgerald says 1776). By then, William Handcock wrote, the citizens were lucky not to depend on it, “for it is so polluted by paper-making that it has become poisonous, and cattle and horses have died from drinking it.”

History · 1240s to the 1960s The mills Seven centuries of water power, from abbey mills to cotton and poplin. In brief For about seven centuries the river turned the wheels of mills for flour, paper, cotton and linen.

The Poddle was bent and diverted above all to turn mill wheels. The monks of St Thomas’s Abbey brought Dodder water into it in the 1240s partly for their mills, and between 1245 and 1324 they redirected its course again to serve them. Archaeology backs this up: a millpond excavated on the Poddle’s bank off New Street was dug in the 13th or 14th century and filled in during the 14th or 15th (Antoine Giacometti, “Blackpitts: Dublin’s medieval tanning quarter”). By 1719 Parliament was complaining that mills along the watercourse were building dams and ponds and starving the city of water.

Mount Down Mill : where the City Watercourse met the Tymon River, upstream of Kimmage. In 1952 its owner, Peter Cullen, sued Dublin Corporation for £20,000 over the mill’s ancient water right, after the Corporation lowered the crest of the city weir. Sources differ on the details: McEntee and Corcoran say he was awarded £20,000 in the High Court in 1952, while Sister Ann Dominica Fitzgerald says the weir was lowered in 1943 and the £20,000 awarded by the Supreme Court in 1960. Ravensdale Mills , Kimmage Road Lower: corn and flour, with a pond, sluice and weir, on maps from the 1830s to 1940. Farrington’s Mill , Kimmage Cross Roads: flour, with a water turbine until the 1920s. Larkfield Mills and a second mill and pond near St Martin’s Drive, with windmills close by. Loader’s Park Mills , Kimmage Road Lower: a corn mill, now the Waterwheel apartments. Mount Argus : a 19th-century paper mill and a flour mill that became a laundry. Harold’s Cross : several watermills, including one in today’s Harold’s Cross Park and a flour mill by Mount Jerome’s gates. Greenmount Mills : a corn mill turned cotton mill by 1807, enlarged by the Quaker Pim family for cotton and linen. Rutland Mill , Rutland Avenue, Dolphin’s Barn: a flour mill on the City Watercourse, run by Clibborn and Shaw. George Carr Shaw, father of George Bernard Shaw, was a partner. Mill Street and Sweeney’s Lane : a double mill for oil and flour linked to St Thomas’s Abbey. Cross Poddle , New Street: a medieval mill beside St Nicholas’ Bridge.

Steam, electricity and competition from British and foreign manufacturers closed the mills one by one in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. Their ponds were filled in and their races culverted. Greenmount’s mill pond was among the last to go, covered over in the late 1960s. Almost nothing is left to see, but the names survive: Mill Street, the Waterwheel, Larkfield. History · 1437 to 2027 Floods and the flood scheme Six centuries of flooding, and the scheme being built to stop it. In brief The Poddle has flooded for six centuries; a scheme now stores water upstream to protect over 800 properties.

The Poddle has always flooded. The cathedral records run from an inquiry in 1437 to boats being rowed past St Patrick’s in 1701. In the suburbs, serious floods struck Harold’s Cross and Kimmage in 1986, 1993, 2000, 2008 and 2011, and Blackpitts flooded during Hurricane Charlie in 1986.

Old newspapers fill in the gaps between the big floods. In March 1787 Faulkner’s Dublin Journal reported that “the river Soulagh (or Poddle, as commonly called) has overflowed the end of New Street, near Kevin Street, to such a degree to make it impassable, so that the folks who pass that way are carried over the stream in Noddies”, the little one-horse cabs of the day. That November the floods came again: Patrick Street “presented a melancholy spectacle”, people from New Street to Bride’s Alley had to live in their upstairs rooms, and the river broke out in the Lower Castle Yard and flooded Crampton Court and Palace Street. In January 1784 melting snow and heavy rain flooded the Liffey, the Dodder and the Poddle together. On 21 February 1910 the Irish Independent reported the Poddle overflowing at Harold’s Cross. On 13 March 1937 the Irish Press described cottages on Rutland Avenue flooded about three feet deep when the culvert at Dolphin’s Barn choked. In December 1954 families behind Fortfield Road in Terenure were forced out of their homes, and on St Swithin’s Day, 15 July 1973, the river flooded two houses at Loder Park beside Mount Argus. In the storms at the end of December 1978 it burst its banks at Templeogue. Dublin Corporation’s minutes also record flooding of the Dodder, the Camac and the Poddle in 1959. Lower Kimmage Road had a particular problem. In November 1985 the Irish Press and the Evening Press reported back gardens collapsing into the river, more were lost in 1987, and the Corporation went to tender in 1986 for about 250 metres of precast culvert to enclose that stretch. The Corporation’s minutes for 1985 to 1987 follow the story, from a report on the river at Kimmage Road Lower and the collapse of the garden of No. 9 into it, to the culverting between Kimmage Road Lower, Harold’s Cross Bridge and Parnell Road, and a report on the 1986 flooding. The newspaper reports are collected by the Crumlin and Walkinstown History Group’s Poddle project. McEntee and Corcoran give the engineers’ side. Jack Keyes’s report of December 1986 called the Hurricane Charlie flood of that August “among the worst on this river since records began”, with 80 homes and 5 businesses flooded, worst at Kimmage Cross Roads, Ravensdale, Mount Argus and Harold’s Cross. At Lower Kimmage Road the river ran in a culvert under the front gardens of more than twenty houses; a long section collapsed in 1985, and Keyes found that only 15 per cent of the river’s course could carry a flood. The front-garden culvert was rebuilt in 1988 and 1989.

On the evening of 24 October 2011, between 80 and 90mm of rain fell on Dublin in six hours. The Poddle burst its banks at Tallaght, Kimmage, Harold’s Cross and Mount Jerome. Across the Dublin region about 1,000 properties flooded, 318 roads were badly flooded, power was lost, and two people died. Both South Dublin County Council and Dublin City Council activated their major emergency plans, and insurance claims were estimated at €127 million. On the Poddle itself, McEntee and Corcoran record, debris blocked the river screens at the Lakelands overflow and the river burst its banks and ran overland; then the screen at Gandon Hall, near Harold’s Cross, blocked too, causing widespread flooding downstream. Eleven places and 113 premises were affected, many cars were written off, and one person died.
The River Poddle Flood Alleviation Scheme

The scheme is a joint project of South Dublin County Council, Dublin City Council and the Office of Public Works, which funds it. It is designed to protect more than 800 properties against a 1-in-100-year flood, with an allowance for climate change. The estimated cost was €7 million in 2020, revised to €10 million by 2023. Its main idea is to store water upstream rather than build high walls in the city. Tymon Lake becomes a flood reservoir behind a 220m embankment and flow-control structure, and Whitehall Park and Ravensdale Park are reshaped to hold water. Downstream, new walls go in at Whitehall Road, Fortfield Road, Poddle Park, St Martin’s Drive and a 25m wall at Mount Argus Close. An integrated constructed wetland in Tymon Park cleans the water, and floating nesting platforms on the lake are for birds.

The scheme has not been uncontroversial. When it was published in 2020, local groups including Save the Poddle’s Wildlife Sanctuary objected to the number of trees to be felled and questioned the bird surveys at Tymon Lake. The Poddle flood scheme was a joint application by South Dublin County Council and Dublin City Council, with the Office of Public Works, to An Bord Pleanála (case 306725). The application includes a planning report, an environmental impact assessment report (EIAR) and a heritage chapter that rewrites the river’s history from the maps and excavations. This page gathers the details that are not on the other pages, from the full documents, which are linked below. It also draws on three Dublin City Council planning applications: the Tenters Blackpitts drawings (2768/09), a mixed-use scheme on Donore Avenue (4156/06) and the Ship Street office and convention centre scheme (4223/18).

The EIAR gives the river’s length as about 11.6 km, and its catchment as about 16.4 km² (16,400 hectares). Its non-technical summary rounds the length to about 10 km. The river rises at Cookstown, north of Tallaght, and flows through Tymon Park, under the M50, past Templeogue, Kimmage, Mount Jerome and Harold’s Cross, and crosses under the Grand Canal before running under the city to the Liffey at Wellington Quay. The lower and middle reaches are heavily urbanised, culverted and partly channelled. Dublin City Council’s presentation on the scheme says the river once powered 52 mills and commercial enterprises along its course, and that it has 15 associated watercourses. The Poddle catchment, with the culverted stretches in red. Figure 1-1, EIAR Volume 2 main report, Nicholas O’Dwyer Ltd, 2019. From the environmental impact assessment report for the River Poddle Flood Alleviation Scheme (An Bord Pleanála case 306725). Open full size

The planning report lists the significant floods as August 1986, June 1993, November 2000, September 2008 and October 2011. On 25 August 1986, Hurricane Charlie seriously affected 80 households and 5 commercial properties from Kimmage Cross Roads to the Grand Canal. In November 2000, 103 mm of rain fell in 48 hours and the banks broke at Kimmage. In June 1993 the river overtopped after rainfall estimated at between a 1-in-100 and 1-in-250-year event, but the flooding was relatively minor. In September 2008, 58 mm fell over 11 hours in Kimmage. The October 2011 flood is the one that led to the scheme. Up to 90 mm fell in six hours, more than the 1-in-100-year level at the gauges. It flooded Our Lady’s Hospice, Greenmount Avenue, Boyne Court and Gandon Close in Harold’s Cross, and the river burst its banks at Ravensdale Park. Over 50 properties flooded.
