The scheme protects against a flood with a 1% chance of happening in any year, and assumes that 60% of the 12 major culverts, and 40% of the others, are blocked. It adds a freeboard of 500 mm to embankments and 300 mm to walls. The report says 921 properties are protected, out of 1,377 at risk, and that more than 200 properties at Whitehall, Mount Argus Road and the Coombe remain at risk of surface-water flooding, which the scheme does not cover. At Tymon Park a flood storage embankment and flow control structure hold back 66,000 cubic metres and limit the flow passed downstream to 748 litres a second, the 2-year flow. An integrated constructed wetland improves water quality, and floating nesting platforms go onto Tymon Lake. At Whitehall Park the channel is realigned and walls are built around the Lakelands overflow. At Ravensdale Park flood walls 1.1 to 1.35 m high create about 800 cubic metres of extra storage. St Martin’s Drive gets a 1.1 m wall, and there are further walls at the back of Fortfield Road and at Mount Argus Close. Flap valves are fitted to every culvert that drains to the river. Manholes are sealed at Poddle Park, Ravensdale Park, St Teresa’s Gardens, Donore Avenue and the National Stadium. More than 50 culverts, weirs and bridges were surveyed from Greenhills Road to Gandon Close, and level alarms and cameras monitor the Lakelands overflow weir, the Wainsfort Manor culvert and Gandon Close. At the planning stage the report listed the lengths of wall as 453 m from Limekiln Road to Wellington Lane, 367 m from Wellington Park to Wainsfort Manor, 245 m from Glendale Park to Kimmage Manor, 255 m at Ravensdale Park, 223 m at Poddle Park and 291 m from Bangor Road to Mount Argus, plus 127 m, 284 m and 135 m of earth embankment at Tymon Castle, Tymon Lake and Whitehall Park. The designs changed before building, so treat these as the application’s figures. The proposed Tymon flood storage embankment (Option 2). Figure 4-2, EIAR Volume 2 main report. Culverts, and where the river comes up

The EIAR’s map study finds that a row of houses on the northern end of Kimmage Road Lower led to the river being culverted there by 1906 to 1909. It comes up again north of Mount Jerome Road, west of Mount Jerome Church, which matches the open stretch on the map. The scheme’s fish survey notes that the culverts have made the lower river impassable to migratory fish, and that the river has limited fisheries value.
The river’s history, from the heritage chapter

The EIAR dates the channel from Balrothery, near Firhouse, to about 1244, with the Firhouse weir possibly as early as the late 12th century. A 1244 inquisition ordered by the justiciar Maurice Fitzgerald looked at how to bring more water to Dublin, and the Dodder weir was enlarged. In 1245 the King directed John FitzGeffrey to finish his hall in the castle and to bring water to it by the summer of 1246. A 1259 inquisition records an agreement between the monks of St Thomas’s and the citizens to make the new watercourse. The report describes the Tongue, today’s Stone Boat, as a wedge-shaped stone pier at the junction of the Poddle and the City Watercourse, which split the flow to regulate the water reaching the city. The City Watercourse was relied on until 1755, when the Grand Canal supplemented the supply, and it was replaced in the 19th century by the Bohernabreena and Vartry reservoirs. It fed cisterns near James’s Street and later the Grand Canal Basin. The name is recorded as “le Poddell” in 1506. Tymon Castle, a 15th-century tower house in Tymon Park, was demolished in 1960, and the site is a recorded monument. The report notes that the Wainsfort Manor Crescent mill, weir and millrace listed in the protected structures record could not be found on historic maps or on the ground. Of 40 archaeological investigations within 250 m of the scheme, several found the medieval watercourses. Test pits at St Teresa’s Gardens found thick, water-laid silts from a medieval watercourse, and two investigations at Ruben Street found the medieval City Watercourse. At Cork Street the south side of the diverted Poddle was exposed. At the Mercy Convent on Cork Street, the remains of tanning boxes were found where the 1866 map shows a tan yard. Closer to the city, archaeologists working at Tenters Blackpitts, off Mill Street, in 2005, 2007 and 2016 found a possible river channel with a medieval organic layer in it, a red-brick culvert that cuts through older cobbling about half a metre below the ground, and the tanneries shown on Roque’s map of 1756, including two de-hairing barrels. The 2007 report says that the middle of the site was heavily disturbed by building the Poddle culvert and its overflow. Heritage assets at the south-western end of the scheme. The official record of the watercourses

The heritage chapter’s appendix reproduces the National Monuments Service record for the City Watercourse. It describes the Tongue, the “wedge-shaped stone” that divided the watercourse of the Poddle and the Dodder, in the words of Weston St John Joyce in 1912. Two thirds of the flow went to the city by way of Greenmount, under the canal at Goodbody’s factory, then to Blackpitts, New Row and Patrick Street, past St Patrick’s Cathedral, and east through Castle Street and Palace Street to Wellington Quay, where it entered the Liffey. The other branch went north at the Tongue to Dolphin’s Barn, and then along an elevated rampart known as the Back of the Pipes, or the Pipes, to the old City Basin near James’s Street. The same record, drawing on H. F. Berry in 1891, says the watercourse was built in the middle of the 13th century, with its head at Balrothery, in Tallaght. It flowed north-east, skirting the churchyard wall at Templeogue, and was joined by the Poddle at Mount Down Flour Mills. From there the two ran as one stream to the Tongue at Kimmage. A large cistern was built around 1670 on or near the ancient reservoir, which is thought to have been west of St Thomas’s Abbey. Berry also wrote about an inquisition of 1258, which the EIAR dates to 1259. Later writers add numbers for the mills. J. Hegarty records that in 1844 Robert Mallet listed 24 mills at work on the Dodder, 12 on the main stream and the rest on the City Watercourse. B. Mac Giolla Phádraig dates the weir at Firhouse to 1254, and says there were 32 mills in 1879, as well as factories, breweries and distilleries on its banks. He also records that a stream taken off the watercourse in Terenure supplied three fishponds. The National Monuments Service gives map references for some of these places. Its Tongue record sits where the Stone Boat is on the map, and a recorded mill site at Harold’s Cross sits beside Greenmount. A watercourse was recorded at Reuben Street, and Donore Castle, a medieval castle mentioned in 1228, is recorded at White Swan Business Park, off Donore Avenue, with no visible trace.
Blackpitts: the culvert on the drawings

The planning drawings for the Tenters development at Blackpitts, lodged with Dublin City Council in April 2009 for BAM Property and drawn by the engineers WYG, include a rare engineering view of the culverts. One sheet is a long section through two existing culverts. In the first, the culvert bed is at about 9.7 metres above Malin Head, its roof at about 11.1 to 11.7, and the ground above at about 11.7 to 12.1, so the culvert lies about two metres down with its roof close to the surface. In the second, the silt was too deep for the survey to find the bed. The proposal reroutes the culvert in a precast concrete box, 1.8 metres wide, with its bed at about 9.65 metres, and the drawings mention underpinning installed under an earlier planning permission (4685/05) to keep an old archway. These show the river as a working piece of drainage under a modern site, about two metres below the street, and match what the archaeologists found a few years later: a brick culvert cutting through older cobbling, and river channel deposits beneath. The 2006 application for a mixed-use development on Donore Avenue, by the engineers Lohan and Donnelly and Collins Maher Martin Architects, shows the culverted Poddle running diagonally across the site, which was then a printing works beside the White Swan Business Park. The drainage drawing marks a strip along the river line “Poddle keep 6 m distance”, and the building is set back from it. New Row South: the culvert and the mill race

The 2019 application for 27 to 29 New Row South, at the junction of Blackpitts and Fumbally Lane (Dublin City Council planning ref 4423/19, for TC Fumbally Properties Ltd), is a hotel and shared-living scheme of 4 to 8 storeys round a protected former laundry building. The Poddle runs under it. The engineers’ report from J.J. Campbell & Associates says the river is enclosed in a culvert along the eastern boundary of the site, with no manholes or access points inside the site. The nearest manhole, on Fumbally Lane, has a cover level of 11.074 m, and the new ground floor is more than a metre higher. The flood risk assessment by JBA Consulting (5 November 2019) says the Poddle is a culverted watercourse along the south-eastern boundary and that the culvert system then runs north-north-east to the Liffey, 50 m west of the Ha’penny Bridge. It uses the Eastern CFRAM model: the site is in Flood Zone C, with a small strip along the southern boundary in Zone B. At the 1% flood the modelled depth is 0.25 m, and 0.5 m at the 0.1% flood, only at the corner of Blackpitts and Fumbally Lane. The modelled 1% flow in the culvert at the node 155 m downstream is 2.26 cubic metres a second. The report says the flooding would come from water surcharging out of the system upstream, where the culvert on Donore Avenue is too small, and running overland to the site from the west. It found no recorded flooding on the site, and notes that the October 2011 flood did not reach it. The engineers agreed the design with Dublin City Council’s drainage department on 12 July 2019 and discussed the culvert with its Flood Projects and Water Framework Directive Division. Their proposal keeps a clear 3 m on each side of the culvert, with a 4 m high corridor above it for an excavator. Three columns on drilled steel-lined piles are proposed where a protected wall bridges over the culvert, and the foundations are designed so that no building load reaches it. Their correspondence says the same approach was used on the neighbouring site, where about 3.7 m of headroom was provided. A local objector argued that 3 m might not be enough given the piling needed, and the planner’s report recorded that concern. The archaeology report from the city archaeologist records that the site lies in the zone of constraint for a Recorded Monument and the zone of archaeological interest. The archaeological impact assessment by Franc Myles (4 November 2019) found the ground floors of three late 17th-century Dutch Billy houses below the present slab, and identified the Poddle culvert and a culverted mill race within the site. The Newmarket and Blackpitts area was developed in the 17th century as a commercial and industrial district, and the report calls the site one of significant industrial heritage. Work down to formation level is to be monitored by an archaeologist, and any deposits above formation level excavated. The planner’s report of 30 March 2020, after further information received on 4 March 2020, recommends a grant of permission with conditions, including drainage conditions.
Ship Street and the Castle: the line through the city

The engineering report for the Ship Street office and convention centre, lodged in 2018 for a site between Ship Street Great and Chancery Lane, has a page on the Poddle. It cites Clair Sweeney’s Rivers of Dublin, which says the river is culverted or piped for about 4 km through the city, and that its exact historic line is not known, although the section through Dublin Castle is well documented. The river ran parallel with Patrick Street, divided into two or more courses down the west and east sides of the street as far as Ross Road and the site of the southern city wall. It then ran along the walls and the castle ramparts, around the Royal Chapel, and out at the Lower Castle Gate at Palace Street and Dame Street. The report also reproduces a map from D. McEntee and M. Corcoran’s study The Rivers Dodder and Poddle: Mills, Storms, Droughts and the Public Water Supply. Boreholes sunk on the site in 2005 found made ground to between 3 and 5 metres below the surface, glacial till down to about 9 metres, and limestone bedrock between 7 and 9 metres down. The application includes a Dublin City Council drainage record map at 1:1000, dated 16 March 2016, showing the sewers around Ship Street, Chancery Lane and Golden Lane. That shows the kind of record the council will supply for a site: the sheet carries a warning that it is supplied from the corporation’s record sheets without prejudice, and that its accuracy must be checked on site. A floodinfo.ie report attached to the Ship Street application, produced on 25 May 2016, lists the floods recorded for the area. For the Poddle and its tributary it shows Limekiln Lane on 24 August 1905, St Claire’s Avenue and Limekiln Lane on 3 September 1931, a tributary at Marrowbone Lane on 21 January 1941, Clanbrassil Street and Mount Jerome at Harold’s Cross in the storm of 11 June 1963 that also flooded Grafton Street and Rathmines, the Poddle in August 1986, and Mount Argus Road and Kimmage Road Lower on 24 October 2011.
Options and the edge of the scheme

The report compares two designs. Option 1 raised walls along the whole river, some of them 2 m or higher: 44 separate defences over 3.8 km, with pumping stations to pass surface-water runoff over the lines. The chosen Option 2 stores water upstream instead, and needs only 27 defences over 1.5 km. The application describes the works as running from Tymon North, Tallaght, to Marrowbone Lane in the city. An Bord Pleanála asked for further information on 17 July 2020, and the applicants answered on 19 October 2020, with new material on natural flood management, Whitehall Park and St Martin’s Drive.

The heritage chapter lists the mills it found on historic maps. They are described on the mill sites page, which now includes Cutlers Mill and its millrace, a flour mill in the Kimmage demesne, Tinker Mill, and the Domville or Mount Down Mill at Templeogue, where the old records say the Poddle met the City Watercourse.

s: Tallaght to Wellington Quay The river that named Dublin The Poddle is the most important watercourse in Dublin city, it provided its water, its defensive moat and powered its mills. It gave the city its name. Poddle.ie traces the course of its history from source to sea, as it defined the Dublin we know today. The Crumlin and Walkinstown Poddle research

Much of the local detail on this site comes from the Poddle River History Project, a volunteer project of the Crumlin and Walkinstown History Group and Crumlin Community Cleanup. Its volunteers gave more than 500 hours to finding, transcribing and sorting newspaper articles, photographs, stories and reports about the Poddle and the City Watercourse, and first published them in October 2024 at the Dublin Festival of History, in Walkinstown Library, with a talk by Cathy Scuffil. Part of the project was funded by the Local Authority Waters Programme. In November 2026 the group generously agreed to bring their research together with poddle.ie, so that the river’s story can be told in one place. Their place histories are now part of the river walk and its meanders, their people are on the Poddle People page, and their newspaper index is on the Media page. Nature Wildlife of the Poddle Otters, bats, herons and a rare orchid: what lives along Dublin’s hidden river. In brief Like most urban watercourses, the Poddle has suffered from pollution, and the councils are working hard to improve it. Sticklebacks and minnows live in the river, otters have moved into its upper reaches since 2020, bats hunt along it, and the lakes at Tymon Park hold swans, herons, egrets and rare plants.

The Poddle at Poddle Park, Kimmage. Photo: O’Dea , CC BY-SA 4.0 The waterfall crossing between the lakes in Tymon Park. Photo: Alan James , CC BY-SA 2.0 Almost everything that has been recorded lives on the open stretch of the river, through Tymon North, Tymon Park, Whitehall Park and Ravensdale Park. From Kimmage down, the Poddle runs mostly in walls and culverts, and very little has been found there. Most of what we know comes from the ecologists who surveyed the river for the River Poddle Flood Alleviation Scheme between 2018 and 2022. Their reports are in the scheme’s planning file, and they are listed at the bottom of this page.

Like most urban watercourses, the Poddle suffers from pollution. When the Environmental Protection Agency sampled it at Priory Road, Kimmage, in 2007, it scored Q3 on the EPA’s scale, which means moderately polluted, and samples taken at four sites in 2020 gave the same score. The small creatures living in the riverbed were the hardier kinds, such as leeches, midge larvae, water hoglice and small snails, rather than the mayflies and stoneflies of the cleanest mountain streams. The city and county councils are working hard to address that. As part of the flood scheme, an integrated constructed wetland is being created in Tymon Park: a series of planted ponds that cleans the water naturally as it passes through, with the aim of bringing it up to a “good” standard. Pollution is an old problem for the Poddle. In the 18th century the mills along its banks had already turned it into what Whitelaw and Walsh called “an immense sewer”, and there are accounts of cattle and horses dying after drinking from it.

A male three-spined stickleback. Photo: Gilles San Martin , CC BY-SA 2.0 The only fish caught when the river was electrofished in August and September 2020 was the three-spined stickleback. There were hundreds at Whitehall Park, but only five to ten at each of the other sites. Inland Fisheries Ireland says minnows live in the river too. There are no trout, salmon or eels. Inland Fisheries Ireland told the engineers that the Poddle is “not a salmonid river”. The 2020 survey found that the gravel beds should suit young brown trout and eels, and said their absence “suggests that there are barriers to fish movement”: the culverts, and the syphon that carries the river under the Grand Canal.

An otter (photographed in Ukraine). Photo: Byrdyak , CC BY-SA 4.0 The otter is the river’s good-news story. In the surveys of 2018 and 2019, the ecologists found “no otter holts, nor any other evidence of otter”. Then in September 2020 a holt was found in Tymon North. A survey in February 2021 recorded 11 signs of otters, including droppings (called spraints) and two holts, one in use. Fish scales from roach were found near Kimmage Cross Roads, possibly left by an otter, but no other signs were found below Tymon North. The ecologists described it as “a natural colonisation of the river by otters”. The Poddle is still a minor otter river. A study of Dublin’s rivers for Dublin City Council found many more signs on the Dodder and the Tolka, and said the Poddle and the Camac “appeared to support far fewer otters”.

A common pipistrelle (photographed in Belgium). Photo: Gilles San Martin , CC BY-SA 2.0 Bats feed along the river and over the Tymon lakes. Surveys in 2018 and 2019 recorded the common pipistrelle, which was active all night, the soprano pipistrelle, including at Mount Argus, and Leisler’s bat, Ireland’s largest. A bat that was probably a Daubenton’s, which hunts insects just above the water, was also picked up over Tymon. Most activity was over the reedbeds at the edge of Tymon Lake. Old trees in Mount Argus Park and the grounds of Kimmage Manor could make good roosts. Badgers have setts in Tymon North. Their exact location is kept out of the reports to protect them. Hedgehogs, pygmy shrews and stoats have been recorded in the surrounding area and may use the river banks, though none were seen in the surveys.

Mute swans and cygnets (photographed in Oxford). Photo: Charles J. Sharp , CC BY-SA 4.0 The Tymon lakes are the best place for birds on the river. Ecologists counted 19 kinds of waterbird there in early 2018, and 2,616 birds over eight visits in the winter of 2021–22. The commonest are black-headed gulls, common gulls, herring gulls, mallard, moorhens, coots, mute swans, tufted ducks, little grebes and teal. Wigeon, shoveler and snipe have also been seen. Mute swans, mallard, coots and moorhens nest around the ponds. In April 2022 a swan was sitting on a nest in the reedbed at the south-east corner of Tymon Lake. The flood scheme’s plans include floating nesting platforms for the lake. Grey herons and little egrets fish in the river and the ponds, and grey wagtails feed along the stream. A water rail was reported in the Tymon reedbeds in the winter of 2021–22, a new record that the ecologists rated of county importance. No kingfishers or dippers were seen, though both live on the Dodder nearby. A grey heron (photographed in Co. Cork). Photo: Ken Billington , CC BY-SA 3.0 A little egret (photographed in Co. Cork). Photo: Ken Billington , CC BY-SA 3.0 A grey wagtail. Photo: Charles J. Sharp , CC BY-SA 4.0 A grey heron (right, at the water’s edge) on the lake in Tymon Park, west of the M50, November 2026. Photo: poddle.ie. Tymon Park used to be an important feeding ground for Brent geese, which fly in from Arctic Canada for the winter: about 1,200 were reported in 2008 and 700 in 2009. Disturbance by dogs has largely stopped this, and only a few have been seen since. An Taisce argued that the flood scheme’s report played them down.

Common frogs and smooth newts probably breed in the ponds at Tymon Park and Mount Argus, although the surveys did not find any. Dragonflies, including the brown rod dragonfly, hunt over the Tymon lakes, and the meadows and reedbeds hold a wide variety of insects.

Flowering rush. Photo: Michel Langeveld , CC BY-SA 4.0 Broad-leaved helleborine. Photo: Gllawm , CC BY-SA 4.0 In the river itself grow watercress, spiked water-milfoil, pink water-speedwell, pondweed and green algae. Around Tymon Lake there are reedbeds of common reed and bulrush, with yellow iris, great willowherb, meadowsweet and purple-loosestrife. The meadow north and east of the lake is rich in wildflowers, including yellow-rattle, selfheal and what is probably a common spotted-orchid. Three rare plants have been found. Flowering rush, which is rare in Dublin, grows in the river below Tymon Lake, and the council has planted more at the Limekiln lakes. Galingale, a tall sedge, grows around Tymon Lake, in what may be its only wild site in Ireland, though it was probably brought in. And four stems of broad-leaved helleborine, a wild orchid, were found on bare ground near Fortfield Road. The woods of Tymon Park are mostly beech, poplar, ash, horse chestnut, willow, maple, sycamore and birch, with wet willow and alder woodland around some of the ponds. Three invasive plants have been recorded: giant rhubarb at Tymon Lake, which has since been removed, a small patch of Japanese knotweed in the north-west of Tymon Park, and Nuttall’s waterweed in the river channel.

These surveys were done for the River Poddle Flood Alleviation Scheme, except where noted. Records are of what the surveyors saw on the days they visited, so other animals and plants may well be there. Over the Easter weekend of 1985 a gang tunnelled from waste ground beside the Dublin Castle wall, crawled through the sewers under Dame Street and cut through a basement wall of the AIB branch. It was the ladies’ toilet. The alarm went off and they fled empty-handed. The news reports of the time don’t name the Poddle, but the river runs under this corner of Dame Street, and the film Dublin’s Hidden Rivers shows the wall in the culvert that the gang tried to use. The river is open to the air through Tymon Park, Whitehall Park and Ravensdale Park, and these are the best places to see it with a class. From Kimmage down it runs mostly in walls and culverts, though you can still follow its route through the streets. Two ready-made school walks give a route, stops, things to look for and activities: School walk Tymon Park About 1.6 km · 1 to 1½ hours The lake, the flood gate and the wetland, on park paths away from traffic. Please plan any visit under your school’s own outings policy. Keep children back from the water’s edge, and never go near culvert openings or grilles.

Is there a gauge on the Poddle?

Not one that publishes live readings. The Office of Public Works runs Ireland’s network of river gauges, and none of its public stations is on the Poddle. The nearest are on the Dodder, the river the monks borrowed water from at Balrothery, and the one the Lakelands Overflow still sends flood water back to. When the Dodder is high after heavy rain on the Dublin Mountains, the Poddle is usually rising too.

For live weather and rain warnings, check Met Éireann’s warnings page . South Dublin County Council and Dublin City Council post flood alerts on their own channels during events.

The flood scheme was designed with a computer model of the river: a hydraulic model that works out how deep and how fast the water runs in floods of different sizes. The model itself isn’t public, but its results are. floodinfo.ie flood maps : the national interactive flood map. Zoom to Harold’s Cross, Kimmage or Templeogue and switch on the river flood extents to see the modelled flood outlines along the Poddle. floodinfo.ie flood plans : the flood risk management plans and the schemes proposed for each area. poddlefas.ie : the flood alleviation scheme’s own site, with the project background and updates. River water quality status, 2016 to 2021 : the EPA’s ecological status for every river, the Poddle included. waterlevel.ie : all the Office of Public Works’ live gauges, with downloads. A 1-in-100-year flood is a flood with a 1% chance of happening in any one year. It is the standard the Poddle scheme is built to.

Mill sites The mills of the Poddle, one by one Nine mill sites, some of them groups of neighbours, from Templeogue to New Street, in order from source to sea. Select a mill marker on the map to land on its entry here. Templeogue Approximate site

Duncan’s 1821 map of Dublin shows Domville Mill at Templeogue, upstream of Kimmage. Old accounts of the City Watercourse say the Poddle joined it at Mount Down Flour Mills. The 1906 to 1909 Ordnance Survey map labels it Mount Down Mill and shows it as disused. Local histories use the mill to mark the end of the Tymon River section, where the City Watercourse joins. In 1952 the Irish Independent reported its owner, Peter Cullen, suing Dublin Corporation for £20,000 over the mill’s old water right; the Crumlin and Walkinstown History Group says the Cullens held it from 1916 to 1969 and dates the demolition to 1973, but Sister Ann Dominica Fitzgerald wrote in the Irish Press on 1 May 1972 that the mill had already been razed. Two mills worked side by side on this stretch. Ravensdale Mills was a corn and flour mill with its own pond, sluice and weir, on maps from the 1830s until 1940. Farrington’s Mill, beside Kimmage Cross Roads, was a flour mill that worked by water turbine until the 1920s. The 1843 Ordnance Survey map also shows Cutlers Mill and its millrace, and a flour mill with a pond in the Kimmage demesne, and the flood scheme’s heritage report says remains of the Ravensdale mill and Cutlers millrace may survive below ground. Ravensdale Park, beside the site, is one of the places being reshaped to store flood water in the flood alleviation scheme. Larkfield Mills and the St Martin’s Drive mill

Larkfield Mills, a mill with its pond, stood where the Sundrive Shopping Centre is now, and the name Larkfield survives in the area. Close by, near St Martin’s Drive, the first Ordnance Survey map shows another mill, a pond and a windmill together. The 1876 map names Tinker Mill and Larkfield Mill in the Brook Lawn and Sundrive Road area. Local histories describe a corn mill on Kimmage Road Lower, and the building survives as the Waterwheel apartments. The flood scheme’s heritage report lists Loader’s Park Mill as a paper mill on the 1906 to 1909 map, south-east of Mount Argus, so the site may have changed use over time. The report finds no significant impact on its millrace. Show on the map → · Street View → Historic: Griffith’s Valuation map of Dublin, mid-19th century Mount Argus Road

In the 19th century there was a paper mill here, and a flour mill on Mount Argus Road that later became a laundry. The Stone Boat, where the river divides, is nearby. Greenmount Mills and the Hospice mill pond

The National Monuments Service records a mill site here. Greenmount was a corn mill that became a cotton mill by 1807 and was enlarged by the Quaker Pim family for cotton and linen. Beside it, a mill pond by Our Lady’s Hospice is shown on the 1910 Ordnance Survey map, and Rev. Myles Ronan’s 1927 map shows a mill pond and a Wood Mill on this part of the river, with the dotted line of an older water course beside them. Greenmount’s mill pond was among the last to disappear, covered over in the late 1960s. The lanes around it now hold small businesses. Show on the map → · Street View → Historic: Rev. An oil and flour mill, linked to St Thomas’s Abbey, which gave Mill Street its name. Mill Street is first mentioned in 1711. By 1830 the street had several tanners and a fancy weaver, and by 1880 five tanners and a parchment maker. A medieval mill beside St Nicholas’ Bridge, outside St Nicholas’ Gate, at the junction of New Street, Patrick Street and Kevin Street. The old Cross Poddle ran beside it. In 1990 an excavation near Patrick Street led by Claire Walsh uncovered the timbers of a 13th-century corn mill. t: Tymon Park: the lake, the flood gate and the wetland
s: School walk · Tymon Park, east of the M50 Tymon Park: the lake, the flood gate and the wetland A short there-and-back walk beside the Poddle in Tymon Park, east of the M50. It takes in a lake full of waterbirds, the new gate that holds back floods and a wetland that cleans the water, all on park paths and away from traffic. Length About 1.6 km there and back Time 1 to 1½ hours with stops Start and finish The Limekiln Road entrance to Tymon Park, by the Lakeside Birds sign Ground Flat park paths and a boardwalk; no roads to cross. Can be muddy after rain. Best for All classes, 1st to 6th In brief This is the upper Poddle, out in the open. Children can see where the river is held back in a storm, how plants clean its water, and some of the birds that live on it, then follow it to the edge of the park on its way to the city, about 10 km away. There is a printable workbook for this walk, Tymon Park River Walk , at three levels from 1st to 6th class, with activities for every stop. Print this walk

The lake and river have deep, steep edges in places. Keep the class on the paths and back from the water, especially at the flow-control structure and on the boardwalk. Don’t visit just after very heavy rain: the lake is designed to rise quickly then, by up to three metres. Tymon Park is a busy public park with dogs, bikes and runners. Agree a meeting point at the start. Please don’t feed bread to the birds, and keep away from nests in spring. Please plan the visit under your school’s own outings policy, and walk the route yourself first: paths and works change.
The blue line is the river: solid where it is open, dotted where it runs underground. The numbers are the stops. River line © OpenStreetMap contributors.

1 Stop 1: The Limekiln lake At the Lakeside Birds sign, in from the Limekiln Road entrance The Poddle flows through this lake. It is one of the best places in Dublin to see waterbirds: surveys for the flood scheme counted 16 to 19 kinds on the Tymon lakes, including mute swans, mallard, coots, moorhens, tufted ducks, little grebes and gulls. Swans, coots and moorhens nest in the reeds. Look for Swans, ducks, coots and moorhens. Herons and little egrets sometimes stand still at the edge, waiting for fish. Try this Use the Lakeside Birds sign to name the birds you can see. Make a tally: which bird is the most common today? Talk about Why might so many birds choose to live here, in the middle of a city? Wildlife of the Poddle → The path along the Limekiln lake in Tymon Park. Photo: Mark Finegan, November 2026. 2 Stop 2: The flood gate The flow-control structure at the east end of the lake This concrete structure with railings is the first finished part of the River Poddle Flood Alleviation Scheme. It came into use on 20 February 2025. In a big storm it lets only a set amount of water through, so the lake fills up behind the raised bank and can rise by up to three metres. The water is let out slowly once the storm has passed, so the streets downstream in Kimmage and Harold’s Cross don’t flood. Look for The raised grassy bank (the embankment) and the opening where the water leaves the lake. Try this Find something about three metres tall, like a lamp post or a tree. Imagine the lake rising that high in a storm. Talk about Homes in Kimmage and Harold’s Cross flooded in 1987, 1993 and 2011. How does holding water back here help them? Floods and the flood scheme → The flow-control structure at the eastern end of the Limekiln lake. Photo: Mark Finegan, November 2026. 3 Stop 3: The wetland that cleans the river The integrated constructed wetland and its boardwalk Like most city rivers, the Poddle carries some pollution, washed off roads and roofs or leaking from drains. The city is working hard to fix that. This wetland, built as part of the flood scheme, is part of the answer. In a constructed wetland, water moves slowly through a chain of shallow ponds full of reeds, and the plants, mud and tiny living things take out much of the dirt before it reaches the river. Surveys found three-spined sticklebacks, a small fish, in the river here. The reeds shelter dragonflies, and on summer evenings bats hunt insects over the reedbeds by the lake. Look for Reeds and bulrushes, ponds at different levels, and the information sign at the start. Try this Walk the boardwalk quietly and listen. How many different sounds can you hear: birds, wind in the reeds, water, traffic? Talk about Why does the water need to move slowly through the wetland to get clean? Tymon on the river walk → The boardwalk through the integrated constructed wetland, Tymon Park. Photo: Mark Finegan, November 2026. 4 Stop 4: The river leaves the park The small footbridge at the east end of the wetland From here the Poddle runs on in a narrow, steep-sided channel past Whitehall, towards Kimmage. Just past Kimmage Manor it begins its first long run underground, and on its way it passes under Harold’s Cross, the Grand Canal, St Patrick’s Cathedral and Dublin Castle before it reaches the Liffey at Wellington Quay. Look for Which way is the water flowing? Look for a grey wagtail, a small grey and yellow bird that bobs its tail by the water. Try this Stand on the bridge and point the way the river is going. Then turn round and point back to the lake, upstream. Talk about The river goes underground in the city. Why do you think people covered it over? Follow the river all the way to the Liffey → The footbridge over the Poddle at the east end of the wetland, Tymon Park. Photo: Mark Finegan, November 2026.

Older classes can follow the river upstream on the other side of the M50, where it runs through a beech wood with small ponds and a weir, and then under the motorway through a pair of arched tunnels. The footbridge over the M50 at the south of the park links the two halves; allow at least another hour. The M50 crossing and Tymon pages have photos of that stretch, and the story of Tymon Castle and the esker, a ridge left by the Ice Age. Back in class, the For teachers page has more ideas, and the workbooks include experiments on mills and floods. Try the Kimmage to Harold’s Cross walk too.

t: Kimmage to Harold’s Cross: the mill road
s: School walk · Kimmage, Mount Argus and Harold’s Cross Kimmage to Harold’s Cross: the mill road A walk down Kimmage Road Lower and Harold’s Cross Road, following the Poddle through the old mill country, past the Stone Boat that split the river in 1245, to the Grand Canal, where the river dives underneath. Length About 3 km, one way Time 2 to 2½ hours with stops Start Ravensdale Park, by Kimmage Cross Roads Finish Harold’s Cross Bridge on the Grand Canal Ground Footpaths along busy roads and short stretches through parks. Cross at pedestrian lights. Short version Stops 3 to 5, from Sundrive Road to Mount Argus: under 1 km, about 45 minutes In brief This is the middle Poddle, where it is in and out of sight. For hundreds of years its water turned mill wheels along this road. Children can find the clues the mills left behind, see the river in a park, and learn how it gets past the Grand Canal. There is a printable workbook for this walk, The Mill Road Walk , at three levels from 1st to 6th class, with activities for every stop. Print this walk

Kimmage Cross Roads, Sundrive Road and Harold’s Cross Road are busy. Cross only at pedestrian lights and keep the class together on the footpath. The flood scheme is building walls and bridges in Ravensdale Park and Poddle Park until 2027. Stay outside any hoardings; some paths may be closed. The river runs between high walls and steep banks. Keep back from railings and never lean over them. Our Lady’s Hospice and Mount Jerome Cemetery are near the end of the walk. Please pass them quietly. Please plan the visit under your school’s own outings policy, and walk the route yourself first: paths and works change.
The blue line is the river: solid where it is open, dotted where it runs underground. The numbers are the stops. River line © OpenStreetMap contributors.

1 Stop 1: Ravensdale Park Off Kimmage Road Lower, just north of Kimmage Cross Roads The Poddle comes out from under the crossroads here. On the first Ordnance Survey maps of the 1830s and 1840s this was Ravensdale Mills, a corn and flour mill with its own pond, sluice and weir, still on the map in 1940. Beside the crossroads, Farrington’s flour mill ran a water turbine into the 1920s, and Mr Farrington was said to be the first person in the area with electric light. Today the park is being reshaped so that it can fill with flood water in a storm, with new walls and a new footbridge. Look for The river channel, and the new flood walls being built. Try this Look at the land around you. Is the park lower or higher than the road? Why would that help it hold flood water? Talk about Why would you build a park that is meant to flood? Ravensdale and Poddle Park → 2 Stop 2: Poddle Park The road named after the river, just north of Ravensdale Park This road is named after the river. Nearby, Larkfield Mills and its pond stood where Sundrive Shopping Centre is now. Another mill and a windmill stood near today’s St Martin’s Drive, and the stump of a windmill survives in St Martin’s Park. Residents have photographed grey herons fishing in the river along this stretch. Look for The street sign. Then look for the river beside the road, and for a heron standing very still. Try this Compare the 1876 map with what you can see now. What has taken the place of the mill ponds? Talk about Why do you think the road was named after the river? The mill sites → Ordnance Survey five-foot map, 1876, showing Larkfield Mill and its ponds. From the River Poddle flood scheme environmental impact assessment report, Chapter 11. 3 Stop 3: The Stone Boat From the bridge on Sundrive Road, looking south Just east of Sundrive Road, a stone shaped like the bow of a boat sits in the river and splits it in two. The first one was built in 1245, when the Norman city of Dublin was short of water. Two thirds of the water stayed in the Poddle; one third went off in a man-made channel, the City Watercourse, to St Thomas’s Abbey and the city’s drinking water. The stone there now is a modern copy on the same design. You can see it from the footpath on the bridge: look over the south side, upstream, and the stone is in the river just below you. Look for The pointed end of the stone facing the current, and the water parting on either side of it. Try this Share out 12 counters, or 12 children, the way the Stone Boat shares out the water. How many go each way? Talk about In 1245 there were no taps. Where did people in Dublin get their water? The Stone Boat → The Stone Boat dividing the flow 4 Stop 4: The Waterwheel The Waterwheel apartments, Kimmage Road Lower These apartments stand on the site of Loader’s Park Mills, a corn mill, and their name remembers its waterwheel. Along this short stretch of the Poddle there were once mills at Ravensdale, Larkfield, Loader’s Park, Mount Argus and Harold’s Cross, grinding corn and flour and making paper and cloth. Look for The name on the building. On the 1843 map, look for the word “Mill”: how many can you count? Try this Hold one hand flat and tilt it. Pour imaginary water down it. Mills were built where the land drops, so the water falls hard on the wheel. Talk about Why do you think so many mills were built close together on such a small river? The mills → Ordnance Survey six-inch map, 1843, from Kimmage towards Harold’s Cross. From the River Poddle flood scheme environmental impact assessment report, Chapter 11. 5 Stop 5: Mount Argus Mount Argus Park and the church of St Paul of the Cross This is the best place on the walk to see the river itself, tumbling over a weir in the park. A flood pond was made here in the 1980s. In the monastery grounds the river once fed a pond and a millrace for a paper mill. The church was built in the 1870s. Saint Charles of Mount Argus, a priest known for healing, lived and died here and is buried in the church. Bats have been recorded here, and the old trees in the park may be where they roost. Look for The weir, and the river disappearing again at the end of the park. Try this Sketch the weir. Draw arrows to show which way the water goes. Talk about The river goes underground again just past the park. Where do you think it comes out? Mount Argus → The Poddle at Mount Argus 6 Stop 6: Harold’s Cross Park The village green where Kimmage Road Lower meets Harold’s Cross Road Harold’s Cross was once a small mill village. The river runs just west of here, out of sight behind the houses, through the grounds of Our Lady’s Hospice and along the edge of Mount Jerome Cemetery. Downstream, Greenmount Mills made cotton and linen, and its mill pond was not covered over until the late 1960s. The park makes a good place to stop for a snack before the last stretch. Look for The cemetery gates on Harold’s Cross Road. Mount Jerome opened in 1836, and the river runs along its eastern side. Try this Count the steps between here and the canal, or time the last stretch, to work out how fast the class walks. Talk about The river flooded Harold’s Cross in 2011. Why might a river that runs in pipes still flood? Mount Jerome → 7 Stop 7: Under the Grand Canal Harold’s Cross Bridge (Robert Emmet Bridge) When the Grand Canal was dug in the 1790s it cut straight across the Poddle’s path. Since then the river has gone underneath it in a siphon: a pipe that dips down below the canal bed and comes up on the far side. In 2003 archaeologists found the river rushing along at least five metres below the ground beside the canal. From here the Poddle runs underground all the way through the Liberties to the Liffey. Look for The canal and the bridge. The river is under your feet, but you can’t see it. Try this Fill a bendy straw or a piece of tubing with water at school and try it: water goes down and comes up again on its own if the far end is lower. Talk about Why didn’t the canal builders just let the river flow into the canal? Under the Grand Canal → How the siphon works. A simplified drawing, not to scale.

From the canal, older classes can carry on along the river’s buried route through the Liberties to St Patrick’s Cathedral, about 1.5 km more, using the St Patrick’s Cathedral page. The Walk the Hidden River workbook covers the city end, from Blackpitts to the Liffey. Back in class, the For teachers page has more ideas, and the workbooks include experiments on mills and floods. Try the Tymon Park walk too.
